title: Glamorgan great Ingram retires for coaching role
description: Glamorgan's South Africa batter Colin Ingram is to retire aged 41 after 11 seasons with the county and will take up a coaching role at Sophia Gardens.
fullText:
Glamorgan's South Africa batter Colin Ingram is to retire at the end of the season after 11 seasons with the county.

The 41-year-old says he will be taking on a coaching role with Glamorgan after 20 years of following his "dream of playing" and having "lived that every day".

Ingram is Glamorgan's longest-serving overseas player of the 21st century and was their top run-scorer in the Championship promotion-winning side in 2025.

He has scored 31 centuries for Glamorgan across the three formats with a career-best of 257 not out, and captained them in T20 cricket in 2018 and 2019.

Ingram made 40 international appearances in limited-overs matches for South Africa, where he represented Free State, Eastern Province and Warriors at domestic level, as well as playing part of the 2014 season for Somerset.

"Throughout my career I've dreamed big, worked hard, made memories, laughed and cried and seen things and places I never thought possible," he said.

"I've had a full crack and left it all out there."

Glamorgan's director of cricket Mark Wallace described Ingram as a "legend" of the club who has "had a lasting impact" on the county.

Bowler Morris set to leave Glamorgan

How new-look Glamorgan are preparing for pro level

The hard-hitting left-hand batter arrived at Sophia Gardens in 2015, quickly becoming a leading part of the team and a fan favourite.

He then played little Championship cricket for a five-year spell because of knee problems and T20 franchise commitments around the world.

Ingram featured in an impressive range of tournaments in Australia, India, Pakistan, the West Indies and the Middle East, as well as his native South Africa and the UK's Hundred competition, for Oval Invincibles.

Ingram, who returned to longer-form cricket in recent years after a successful knee operation, described cricket as his "art".

"I was fascinated by the game from a young age, and in particular batting," he said in a social media post announcing his retirement.

"At times, when it flows everything slows down and it feels like the most natural, instinctual thing I've ever done.

"Like my form of art and the bat my paint brush and it's exhilarating."

This season he scored centuries against Yorkshire and Warwickshire in the Championship and played a leading role in the home win over Surrey with 80 and 61 not out, but made only three limited-overs appearances.

He could return for a final farewell alongside fellow retiring stalwart Chris Cooke, 40, in the closing Championship match against Essex.

Ingram has an amazing county record of 5645 runs in first-class cricket averaging 47, plus 2630 runs at an average of 62 in one-day matches, and 3431 at 32 in T20 games.

He also took 67 wickets bowling leg-spin, mainly in limited-overs matches, and filled in as an occasional wicket-keeper.

On his future plans the South African said:

"As one chapter closes the next opens beyond the boundary as I begin my coaching career.

"My art is complete but I hope to influence the game positively and inspire players to be the best they can while enjoying their journeys."

Director of cricket Wallace said: "Colin Ingram is a Glamorgan legend. His performances, his leadership, and his character have had a lasting impact on this club.

"He has been central to our progress over the last 11 years, and his influence will continue through his new coaching role.

"We thank him for everything he has given to Glamorgan and look forward to seeing him shape the future of our playing group."

title: 'This is not Wrexham. I'm not Ryan Reynolds' - behind the scenes at world's oldest club
description: A new BBC podcast Mud, Sweat and Cheers: Trouble at the Bottom – Sheffield FC goes behind the scenes on an extraordinary season at the world's oldest football club.
fullText:
A football club at the heart of a tug-of-war between a Qatari-backed venture capital firm and a rock star probably isn't that unusual nowadays.

This is the position that Sheffield FC, founded in 1857 and widely considered the world's oldest football club, were in earlier this year.

Mud, Sweat and Cheers: Trouble at the Bottom – Sheffield FC, a six-part podcast series from BBC Local and BBC Radio Sheffield and hosted by Sheffield singer-songwriter Self Esteem, goes behind the scenes during an extraordinary season for an extraordinary club.

The Club, as they're aptly nicknamed given their historic place in the sport, helped to underpin many of the laws of the modern game with the 'Sheffield Rules' and are one of just two clubs to have been awarded Fifa's prestigious Order of Merit, alongside 15-time European Cup winners Real Madrid.

Interest in the club from Qatar isn't actually anything new, a delegation from the country visited in 2017 in the build up to hosting the 2022 World Cup.

Despite Yorkshire AI Labs, backed by money from the Middle East country, saying they had plans to build a 15,000-seat stadium and a football museum it was Jon McClure, lead singer of Sheffield indie band Reverend and the Makers, who became chairman in March.

McClure is honest and up front about the goals for a club who might be the oldest in the world but have never played in the Football League and whose best FA Cup runs were reaching the fourth round in 1879 and 1880.

"This is not Wrexham. I'm not Ryan Reynolds. Let's get it clear, I'm in an indie band. I know my place in this world," McClure told BBC Radio Sheffield in March.

"I've taken a lot of advice from football people. I'm not a football person, and I won't be involved in football stuff."

In recent years Hollywood actors Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac have helped Wrexham soar through the divisions from the National League up to the Championship.

This might not be Wrexham but McClure, who has also taken over at the club's women's side who play in the fourth tier, has plans for a football academy, eSports hub, national football festival, clothing brand, visitor centre, TV show and getting the club back playing in the city of their and the wider game's birth.

Since 2001 they have played at the Coach and Horses Ground (behind, unsurprisingly, the Coach and Horses pub) in Dronfield, North Derbyshire.

The ground's seen better days, with one female supporter telling the podcast the women's toilets are "disgusting".

"I think everybody wants the club back in the city, but there's only Sheffield that could invent football and build a B&Q car park on it," McClure says in relation to the site of their original home now being occupied by a DIY shop.

With the Club challenging to go up from the United Counties League Premier Division North at the back end of the 2025-26 campaign McClure offers free entry to under-16s to try and boost the atmosphere.

"We're pushing for promotion. Obviously, we've got this under-16s come for nowt," he says.

"They're good kids. I've said to them overnight, 'listen, lads, we need more noise out of you'.

"They were a bit quiet. So I said, 'look, if you bring a drum, I'll buy you all a pie'. So I owe them all a pie. Well, a fair trade's no robbery, is it?"

However as good as McClure's intentions might be, not everyone is delighted with the new fans.

One complains about the abuse of players and an announcement is read out over the Tannoy at one game asking them to "refrain from throwing drinks" after a supporter is drenched in lemonade.

The push for an immediate return to the eighth tier is spearheaded by striker Alex Hardwick.

Off the field, Hardwick, like the rest of his team-mates, has another job. His though is a little more unusual than others.

"I'm a design engineer here at the AMRC (advanced manufacturing research centre). I work in a design and prototyping building. I work on a range of different projects, which range from nuclear to automotive," he says.

When he isn't busy with his day job or plundering goals, Hardwick is always willing to help out if one of the lads has an issue with their car and adds that a couple of them "do not know their way around an engine".

Boss Vill Powell acknowledges Hardwick "brings a different dynamic to the dressing room, in terms of his conversation, in terms of his banter, in terms of how he is in general".

Watching on from the stands, hopefully not soaked in lemonade, his grandparents are his number one fans.

"I just love it. I enjoy it. I get disappointed when he can't get a goal," his grandma says.

"We encourage him all the time. I don't disappoint him. Marks out of 10? Yeah, I give him 9.5," his grandad adds.

McClure feels that the Club and the city itself have not done enough to celebrate their role in the history of football.

"For far too long now this city has not shouted about itself. It's enough now," he said.

"Now's our time to stand up and say this city's brilliant.

"We invented this game, and this club invented this game, and we're going to celebrate that."

It's a sentiment shared by the fans, with one saying "if the first club in the world was based in Manchester, it would be all over everywhere. If it was in London, it would be all over everywhere. We do nothing about it" while another adds "I certainly believe Sheffield Club should be held in higher esteem".

Like anyone involved in football management and administration one thing McClure wants more than anything else now is something the world's oldest football club knows all about. Time.

Upon taking over he said: "Judge it in a year. If it's not tangibly in a better place than it is now, come and see me at a match and discuss why you think that's not the case."

title: What's gone wrong at Lancashire?
description: Lancashire are set to end 2026 in the bottom two of Division Two, their lowest-ever finish in the County Championship.
fullText:
With one match of the 2026 season remaining, unwanted history beckons for Lancashire.

This proud county is staring at the lowest finish in their 136 years of competing in the Championship. They are seventh in Division Two and could finish bottom.

Never before have Lancashire ended a season either 17th or 18th position out of all the first-class counties, but after a miserable summer of red-ball cricket, it is now staring them in the face.

They begin the final round of games nine points above bottom side Gloucestershire, but it would be little surprise if Lancashire, who welcome runaway Division Two champions Durham starting on Thursday, were overtaken and ended up bottom of the pile given how the last few months have played out.

So how has it gone so wrong for one of English cricket's traditional powerhouses?

Since the launch of the two-tier system in 2000, Lancashire had previously spent only three years in Division Two, bouncing back to the top flight as champions at the first time of asking on each occasion.

But following a fourth relegation two years ago, things have been far from straightforward in the second tier.

Expecting a quick turnaround, head coach Dale Benkenstein left the club halfway through the 2025 season after Lancashire started with no wins from their opening seven Championship games.

Just before his own departure, Benkenstein had talked about a lack of clarity , externalwithin the club about whether the priority was to produce a winning team or to bring through young players. Fast forward over 12 months and that perceived issue has not been resolved.

Former player Steven Croft took over in an interim role from the South African and with three wins from the second half of the season with improved cricket and morale, he was handed the head coach job permanently.

With England legend James Anderson taking on the captaincy on a permanent basis for 2026, the hope was Lancashire would be challenging for promotion this year.

That certainly looked the case as the Red Rose won two and drew one of their first three matches, as Anderson took 21 wickets, including a match-winning 4-18 against Derbyshire.

However, a victory over Gloucestershire in Bristol was one that came at a heavy price as opener Luke Wells and new quick bowler Ajeet Singh Dale picked up injuries that turned out to be season-ending.

From that point in mid-April, the wheels have fallen off in a big way. Lancashire have proceeded to lose eight of the next 10 Championship matches, with the other two being rain-affected draws.

And it is in batting where the Red Rose's flaws have been primarily exposed.

Lancashire have posted one batting bonus point from the past nine matches - a total of 281-8 declared against Worcestershire in May - the only time a first innings score has ticked past 250.

Since the Championship resumed at the end of August, Lancashire's highest total in nine completed first and second innings is 192, with teenager Rocky Flintoff's 65 the highest individual score.

There have only been three Championship centuries all season and collapses have become commonplace, meaning the end-of-year batting averages are going to make for gruesome reading.

Take the last match against Kent. Openers Michael Jones and Jennings battled through the whole morning session on the opening day without losing a wicket, yet within 20 minutes of the restart after lunch, Lancashire had fallen from 81-0 to 82-4 and eventually lost all 10 wickets in the session to be all out for 161.

With the ball, no side has collected more bowling points than Lancashire, while Anderson and George Balderson are two of only six Division Two bowlers to take 50 wickets or more and the only ones in the same side.

But with not enough runs to play with, it has been hard to put opposition teams under serious and lasting pressure.

27 April: Durham (a) - LOST by eight wickets

10 May: Middlesex (h) - LOST by six wickets

18 May: Worcestershire (h) - Match drawn

14 June: Kent (h) - LOST by 140 runs

21 June: Derbyshire (a) - LOST by nine wickets

23 August: Northants (h) - LOST by 316 runs

30 August: Worcestershire (a) - Match drawn

4 September: Middlesex (a) - LOST by 160 runs

11 September: Gloucestershire (h) - LOST by 105 runs

17 September: Kent (a) - LOST by seven wickets

Lancashire's title success in 2011 is their only sole Championship win since 1934, but that should not hide the fact that they remain one of English cricket's biggest teams, able to call upon far superior resources to most of the other sides in county cricket and certainly those in Division Two.

That only makes the paucity of current performances worse and the mood around Emirates Old Trafford is dark.

Many of the club's members are unhappy at how they believe cricket has been secondary in recent years to concerts and conferences and more attention diverted towards Manchester Super Giants in The Hundred.

Chief executive Daniel Gidney is stepping down, with Richard Kenyon arriving from Nottinghamshire to replace him while West Indies great Clive Lloyd has become the new club president and former captain and coach Mike Watkinson has been voted on to the board - with the hope of bringing cricketing expertise to fruition.

And significant change is set to happen this winter after Lancashire announced on Monday the departure of director of cricket performance Mark Chilton, the sign that things must improve on the field, with Gidney referencing the Championship as being at the heart of the club's 'cricketing vision', external.

Remarkably, Lancashire have only won two red-ball matches in four seasons at Old Trafford and fans have watched their team be out-performed on home soil in all three disciplines by Northants and Gloucestershire recently.

Confidence in the team is low and head coach Croft knows it is a tough time for all concerned.

"You don't want to go through this as a player but usually you come out of it a better player," he told BBC Radio Lancashire after the three-day loss at Kent in the last round.

"Then you don't take it for granted when it is going well. But it's a horrible place to be in, as a team as a well as individuals, we're not really clicking.

"Four-day cricket is tough. It's a competitive division, some tricky surfaces, some of the lads have to problem-solve on the job, but that's what it's about to be a good four-day side."

Scott Read, BBC Radio Lancashire commentator

The numbers are well documented, and they don't make for pretty reading. Lancashire have not made 200 in any innings since June, their last batting point came in May and not since April have they managed to pick up more than two batting points.

Since their last win in April against Gloucestershire, they have lost eight of the following 10 Championship matches.

Lancashire have never finished bottom of the County Championship; it's a fate that they will probably avoid even though bottom club Gloucestershire have managed more wins heading into the final round of games.

It's the match against Gloucestershire in Bristol where things started to go wrong this year, season-ending injuries for Ajeet Singh Dale and Luke Wells in the same game deprived them of a new marquee signing and their opening batter.

In fact, they've used seven different opening partnerships this season, their first stand of 50 for the first wicket didn't come until September. Only two players have scored a century, Marcus Harris has done it twice with Paul Coughlin batting at eight being the other.

They've used 25 different players, it's been that kind of season.

Yes, the numbers don't make for pretty reading, at least those numbers don't. In the middle of all this is a remarkable display of endurance, fitness and sheer desire to play which has seen James Anderson miss only two red-ball games.

He's captained and carried the side all summer, ending the season with over 50 wickets. Not since 2005 has Anderson taken 50 wickets in a season for Lancashire. George Balderson has also passed 50 this year, the first time in his career he's reached that milestone.

The club continue to try to give younger players a chance - Rocky Flintoff, Arav Shetty, Joe Moores and Ben Walkden all featuring. But it's 15 years ago that Lancashire last won the title, it's over a decade since they last won major silverware.

And, since finishing second in Division One in 2022 the Red Rose have only won 11 of the following 55 Championship matches, with a relegation in 2024 and are now set for a third successive season in Division Two.

Cricket has a wonderful habit of making fools of us all, it can quickly prove us all wrong, but the trend is worrying and the fear among many members is that it may take some time to turn the fortunes of this famous old club around.

title: Olympic champion Smith to come out of retirement

fullText:
Double Olympic swimming champion Tatjana Smith is coming out of retirement with the aim of competing at the 2028 Los Angeles Games.

The 29-year-old, who is South Africa's most decorated Olympian, said she was "missing the water", adding her return "feels a little crazy, a little scary and very exciting all at once".

Smith, who won 100m breaststroke gold and 200m silver at the Paris 2024 Games, to add to 200m breaststroke gold and 100m silver at Tokyo 2020, is aiming to compete over a new Olympic distance of 50m.

"It's definitely a new challenge, a new event, a new race, but also a new me," she said.

"For the first time, I am choosing swimming and I am choosing the event and I am choosing a new event, that has no history but to try and write some new history.

"LA 2028 is the goal. It is not a promise. I still have to build a race, qualify and earn my place back on those blocks."

title: Egan's late career resurgence back to Premier League
description: BBC Sport NI looks at Republic of Ireland centre-back's John Egan's rise back to the Premier League with Hull City and the international set-up under Heimir Hallgrimsson.
fullText:
Just 18 months ago a 31-year-old John Egan was struggling for minutes off the bench for promotion-chasing Burnley and decided to make a January switch to fellow Championship side Hull City.

Fast forward to the present day and Egan is a Premier League regular for the Tigers, who have taken everyone by surprise upon their return to the top flight.

It's been quite a turnaround for the now 33-year-old, who probably thought his last Premier League appearance had already come, when he was taken off on a stretcher with a season-ending Achilles injury when playing for Sheffield United against West Ham in September 2023.

Egan has quietly rebuilt his career after being released by the Blades, first with the Clarets before finding a home at Hull after joining in 2024.

He signed a new two-year deal earlier this month, has played five of their league games and has even forced his way back into the Republic of Ireland squad.

His late career resurgence back to the Premier League is a story of perseverance and unwavering belief despite considerable adversity.

Hallgrimsson spoke to players individually about Israel games

Coleman not included in Republic of Ireland squad

Egan made 208 appearances for Sheffield United during his six seasons with the club, winning promotion to the Premier League with them in 2019 and 2023.

He was named club captain in the summer of 2023, but would play his last game for the Blades in September that same year as an Achilles injury curtailed his Premier League return and kept him out for close to 10 months.

The defender's contract expired the following summer and the club decided not to renew the deal, leaving Egan hurt and in the lurch as he tried to battle back from that serious injury and continue his career.

He went on trial to Burnley and West Ham, with then Clarets boss Scott Parker seeing enough from the experienced centre-back to offer him a one-year deal with the club seeking a quick return to the top flight after relegation the previous season.

With Burnley then getting off to a flying start in the Championship, Egan, who was working back to full fitness, was restricted to just seven appearances and decided to swap a promotion push at Turf Moor for a relegation battle with Hull just five months later.

He signed an 18-month deal and was thrown straight in, completing his first 90 minutes in over a year, coincidentally against Burnley in a 2-0 loss in February.

The Kerry native would go on to make 10 more appearances as Hull stayed up on goal difference on the final day.

Manager Sergej Jakirovic then came in and transformed the club the following campaign, with a fully-fit Egan a key player in their success.

He played 48 times as Hull sneaked into the play-offs and then beat Middlesborough in the final to return to the Premier League for the first time since 2017.

Egan picked up where he left off last season in the top flight this term, as evidenced by his performance in the opening day 2-0 victory over Manchester United.

He made 18 clearances against the Red Devils and has since helped the Tigers keep clean sheets against Coventry and Aston Villa before they earned a point against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge and lost narrowly against Newcastle.

It's been a dream return to the top flight for Hull and Egan, who have shown they are up for the fight in the battle to stay in the league.

Egan's form at Hull helped him to earn an international recall with the Republic of Ireland in October last year, after two years without a call-up.

Previously an automatic starter, the rise of the likes of Nathan Collins, Dara O'Shea and Jake O'Brien have pushed him down the pecking order and he has played a bit-part role under Heimir Hallgrimsson.

Egan came off the bench for the closing stages of the 1-0 defeat against Portugal and was then on the bench for the subsequent wins against Armenia, Portugal and famously Hungary, which gave them a shot at the World Cup via the play-offs.

He again was an unused substitute in the heartbreaking shootout defeat against Czech Republic before winning his 38th cap by starting in a 0-0 friendly draw against North Macedonia in May.

With Hallgrimsson's preference for playing with three centre-backs, Egan has certainly staked a claim for occupying one of those slots in the Nations League opener against Kosovo given his start to the season.

His case is strengthened by the fact that captain Collins is out injured, O'Brien has been limited to three appearances for Everton and O'Shea has been playing out of position at right-back for Ipswich Town.

The other centre-back options in the squad - new call-up Liam Kitching, Jimmy Dunne and James Abankwah - are inexperienced on the international stage.

Even if he does not start in Pristina, the condensed nature of the window and with a game against Austria sandwiched between two against Israel in 12 days, he is sure to see some game time for his country.

Given what he has gone through just to make it back to the top flight and into the Irish squad, Egan will fancy his chances of re-establishing himself as a starter for country as he did at club level.

Joao Pedro spares Chelsea blushes in home draw with Hull

title: McPake's 'colourful' journey from club-less to Scotland call-up in three years
description: Three years ago, Josh McPake was without a club. Twenty months ago, he was in the shop window but "no-one wanted him". This week, he's involved in his first Scotland camp. Here, BBC Sport Scotland charts the fall and rise of the winger who's got everyone in the country talking.
fullText:
Three years ago, Josh McPake was without a club. Twenty months ago, he was in the shop window but "no-one wanted him".

This week, he's involved in his first Scotland camp following a heroic start to life at Hearts, where, to the tune of Abba's Dancing Queen, the supporters sing he is "having the time of his life".

His call-up to Sebastien Poconogli's squad for the upcoming Nations League games caps an eventful few years for the 25-year-old winger.

From Rangers academy's next big thing, to dropping into Scottish League 1 with Stirling Albion, to being shelved at St Johnstone, it's been a colourful - and at times chaotic - career so far.

But, "I wouldn't change my journey for anything," McPake insists.

He now appears at home in Gorgie and many have hopes he will be just as comfortable when he gets the opportunity to represent his country.

His story is one of resilience and patience. And it's paying off.

BBC Sport Scotland charts the fall and rise of McPake as "he can pass, he can score, having the time of his life, Josh McPake, watch him play on a Saturday".

Sesko among three injury absences for Slovenia against Scotland

Scotland call for Montgomery as Tierney & McLean drop out

How is Scotland squad shaping up for Pocognoli debut?

Pocognoli Facetime helps Miller over summer of discontent

His story starts like many others, in the Ibrox academy from a young age, where he was awarded player of the year in 2019 by working up through the reserves to the fringes of the first team.

A matter of months after collecting the gong, he was given his first - and only - run-out for Steven Gerrard's side.

His appearance off the bench in Rangers' rout against Gibraltar's St Joseph's in Europa League qualifying was not a sign of things to come, as he was sent out on his first of six loan moves just one month later.

Dundee, Greenock Morton, Harrogate Town, Morecambe, Tranmere Rovers and Queen's Park all had a taste of McPake but nothing permanent was made.

He swiftly became a bit of a football nomad.

While on Tayside, he scored the winner for Scotland Under-19s against Germany, but still he was flung from pillar to post.

On 1 September 2023, he left Rangers and, though he trained with a number of clubs - where he endured some "knocks and setbacks" - he didn't find a home for another near-six months, until Stirling signed him on a short-term deal.

A dunt down to earth, no doubt, but McPake didn't allow any ego to get in his way, as then-Binos boss Darren Young recalled.

"He came into training and he was brilliant - he couldn't have done any more," former Aberdeen midfielder Young told BBC Scotland.

"He worked very, very hard. He helped put balls away after training, he was always doing extra bits of shooting and finishing - I joked to him once or twice, 'if you don't get your finger out then you'll end up back here part-time' but it was one of those where you could see his ability, he was head and shoulders above the guys.

"It was just a case of him then doing it and getting into the kind of situation where a club - and the right club - would come and get him."

He scored on his debut for the League 1 side - though that was little surprise to Young who was left "wondering why he had not been signed up" when he got the move in motion.

"We had an eye on him as he was free but it looked like he was going to sign at a higher level but another player got injured and then the move wasn't going to happen," he explained.

"He sort of found himself in limbo but I think there's a lot of positives that can be learned from that.

"He kind of said, 'well, I don't want to be in this position and I don't want to be back down there again' and the only way to do that is by working hard and working on weaknesses, which he did."

It'll be of no surprise McPake didn't lack anything in the attacking sense. A wee bit of fine tuning on his tracking back was all that was required during his time at Forthbank to fire him back to where he wanted to be.

"I didn't need to tell him how to go by a player and put it in the top corner - he had all that," Young said.

"I was just trying to say if he could fit into the structure here, work as hard at going back as he did forward, then he'd get, hopefully, an opportunity to kick on again.

"Some players don't, some players kind of have that attitude of, 'I can do it going forward, I don't need to do it going back,' but the penny dropped and he realised to improve and progress, that's what he had to add.

"He worked hard for it and he's got what he deserved."

The reward for knuckling down - and dropping down - was a move back to the top flight with St Johnstone - despite suffering relegation with Stirling Albion.

A two-year deal was agreed but he failed to force his way into Craig Levein's team, and had similar struggles when Simo Valakari took over in October 2024.

His mettle was being pushed to the max yet again.

The Finn revealed last year, external that McPake was made available in the winter transfer window while Saints were fighting for their Premiership life, but they "couldn't find him any clubs".

"We made Josh available in January and offered him to many clubs because he needed to play," Valakari said.

"The truth is, nobody wanted him. We couldn't find him any clubs.

"And, for me, that was the wake-up call for Josh. That was when he decided things had to change.

"If things had stayed the way they were then football was done for him. He would have had to go and get a normal life."

What followed was far from normal.

McPake started his first Premiership game for St Johnstone in the first of their five post-split games and kept his place until the end of the season as he registered three assists.

Saints were ultimately relegated but it set him up for the season of his dreams.

He set the tone for the Championship campaign he dominated with a hat-trick on the opening weekend against title rivals Partick Thistle.

In the second tier, his blistering pace, immense physicality and dancing feet were flung back into the spotlight. His eye for a goal - 16 all told in the division - was evident, too.

Such qualities caught the attention of then Premiership leaders Hearts, who agreed a pre-contract back in January.

But there was no head-turn from the winger, who remained fully focused on repaying the club who resurrected his career by ensuring they would be an opponent of his this season.

He ended the campaign with the mantelpiece packed with trophies and, while the personal accolades were appreciated, it was all about the Championship winners' medal for Tynecastle-bound McPake.

Ensuring adversity remained an ever present in his tale, the footballing gods - seemingly - threw another curveball McPake's way.

Though Derek McInnes was in charge when he agreed the move, the head coach had headed for Rangers by the time he got going in Gorgie.

But, despite sitting out the Champions League qualifiers against Sturm Graz and the first league game of the season under Wouter Vrancken, the Belgian has quickly found out why Hearts snapped up the Saints showman when they did.

With eight goal involvements in 11 games - his best contribution a goal and assist in the Edinburgh derby - he has made the step back up to the Premiership a seamless one and, as such, made it nigh impossible for Pocognoli to leave him out of his plans.

"I've loved every part of the journey," McPake said after answering his country's call.

"Personally, I feel I needed those experiences to become the player I am now.

"There were a lot of setbacks but going down the levels, proving myself and working my way back up taught me a lot.

"If you want something enough and work hard for it, you can achieve it.

"I don't want to stop here. I feel I've still got more to give and I'll continue working hard to show what I can do."

title: 'I'm an idiot' - Strickland survives crash with no helmet
description: UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland says he is "OK" but "an idiot" after surviving a crash in an off-road vehicle while not wearing a helmet.
fullText:
UFC middleweight champion Sean Strickland says he is "OK" but "an idiot" after surviving a crash in an off-road vehicle while not wearing a helmet.

In a series of posts on Instagram, Strickland describes the crash as happening at 60mph with the vehicle rolling "around six times".

The 35-year-old American says he was a passenger in the vehicle alongside his friend Chris Cornell, who was driving.

Strickland says Cornell was taken to hospital after falling unconscious, before later posting a picture of him with his thumbs up in a hospital bed alongside an X-ray of a broken bone.

Strickland did not confirm if he went to hospital.

In footage posted after the crash, Strickland shows grazes on his head and back, before describing himself as an "idiot" for not wearing a helmet.

"Guys I'm in a real bad place. I let my buddy drive, he rolled us going like 60 (mph), we rolled like six times," said Strickland.

"That's from my head smacking the ground going 60. I didn't have a helmet on, I'm an idiot."

Strickland, who lives in Las Vegas, did not say where the crash took place, but a video posted shortly before the accident shows the UFC fighter in the desert before he went riding.

Strickland later posted an update, saying he is "a little concussed but good and wants to spar tomorrow".

"Think I'm OK, Chris is in the hospital but I think he's going to be alright," he added.

"It was the most fun I've had in a long time. My shoulder's a little sore."

Strickland is a polarising figure in MMA and has made homophobic and racist remarks as well as derogatory comments about women.

He became a two-time UFC middleweight champion by beating Khamzat Chimaev in May.

title: Red Bull's Hadjar to return at Azerbaijan Grand Prix
description: Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar will return at this week's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.
fullText:
Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar will return at this week's Azerbaijan Grand Prix after missing the past three races with a wrist injury.

The 21-year-old Frenchman was replaced by New Zealand's Liam Lawson for races in the Netherlands, Monza and Madrid after injuring his wrist while boxing.

In statement, Red Bull said Hadjar has made a "full recovery" and will replace Lawson for the Grand Prix in Baku, which runs from 24-26 September.

"The team would like to sincerely thank Liam for his professionalism, dedication and hard work over the past three races," Red Bull added.

"Stepping in under challenging circumstances, he delivered some impressive performances and made a valuable contribution to the team."

Lawson, 24, finished seventh in Zandvoort and sixth in Madrid but failed to score a point at Monza after coming 14th.

After being replaced by Hadjar, Lawson will return to Red Bull's junior team Racing Bulls.

Hadjar, who will return to action alongside four-time world champion Max Verstappen, is eighth in the drivers' standings having scored 71 points this season.

title: 'Alarming' - does WSL have a homegrown problem?
description: The London City Lionesses raised eyebrows with no English players in their starting line-up against Manchester United, but is there a wider trend?
fullText:
When London City Lionesses beat Manchester United on the opening night of the 2025-26 season, it suggested times were changing in the English women's game.

For some, that had become clear about an hour before kick-off in Bromley when the team news revealed a starting XI without any English players - the first time a Women's Super League side had done so on the first day of the season.

Two days later it happened again, when Scotland striker Kirsty Hanson was the only British player to start for Tottenham in their win over West Ham.

Both instances speak to the increasing ability of WSL clubs to attract top talents from across the globe, creating a league many now view as the world's best.

But, with the Women's Champions League returning this week, is what's good for the WSL good for homegrown players, and by extension the home nations?

Or is it, as The Guardian's Tom Garry puts it, "alarming" for the hopes of the home nations?

Arsenal v HB Koge, Women's Champions League

Tuesday, 22 September, 20:00 BST

Listen to BBC Radio 5 Live commentary and follow text updates of the matches featuring English teams on the BBC Sport website as the Women's Champions League returns

Ten years ago when current champions Manchester City last won the WSL title, they did so with an all-British starting line-up.

In 2018, the WSL went fully professional, the subsequent success of the Lionesses in the 2020s rapidly grew the game's audience and revenues have increased accordingly.

As a result, clubs have expanded their scouting pool and been able to attract players from a wider variety of nationalities - with transfer fees exploding since the turn of the decade.

Over recent windows, WSL clubs have recruited heavily from Germany and Sweden, while two-time Ballon d'Or winner Alexia Putellas exchanged the trophies of Barcelona for big-spending London City this summer.

The proliferation of players from Japan and Australia also highlights the WSL's attractiveness for those at the top of the game as those clubs with the deepest pockets pack their squads with players from across the globe.

"Our league has grown significantly and attracted world class athletes from all over the world," says Birmingham City manager Amy Merricks. "Unfortunately that blocks some of the pathways for the youngsters coming through.

"We need [this] talent in our league because our league is growing, but at the same time we have got to try and address this issue."

Looking at the proportion of homegrown players (English, Scottish, Welsh and Northern Irish) to start 11 or more matches, half of a WSL season, the data shows a steady decline over the past three seasons to under a third.

The first three weeks of 2026-27 have offered a bump on last season, but that can partly be attributed to the WSL's expansion from 12 teams to 14 teams and the greater proportion of homegrown talent in the promoted trio of Birmingham City, Crystal Palace and Charlton Athletic.

It is a downward trend that is not mirrored across other major European leagues.

For 2025-26, 61% of those to start half or more of Premiere Ligue matches in France were French, 63% of those in Frauen Bundesliga games were German, and 69% of Liga F players in Spain were Spanish.

And, while WSL managers say they appreciate the importance of cultivating homegrown talent, the reality of the job ensures it is not their first priority.

"The club has a responsibility to raise young players, give our own talents possibilities to be in the squad and compete every week," says Manchester City boss Andree Jeglertz.

"But when it comes to team selection, I always need to pick the team that gives us the best chance of winning the game. If that contains eight young and promising English players or zero, I don't care. I just want to win the game."

Ellen White and Ben Haines discuss homegrown WSL players on the Women's Football Weekly

Superstar-led London City live up to hype as Man Utd suffer

It feels like a crossroads has been reached between clubs wanting to be competitive, the WSL continuing to grow, and the need to regenerate an England squad that has not changed much over the past three major tournaments.

After all, England are the two-time European champions but seven of the team that started against Spain in June also played in the Euro 2022 final against Germany - while two of the remaining starters in this year's game were on the bench four years ago.

Sarina Wiegman's side were outclassed in Majorca, losing 4-0 to miss out on automatic qualification for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil. They must now navigate two rounds of play-off matches, starting against Greece next month.

Discussions on England's future is pertinent given the biennial Women's Under-20s World Cup is ongoing in Poland.

Last Thursday, Lydia Bedford's young side were dismissed 3-0 from the last 16 by Nigeria, albeit with the caveat a number of players such as US-based Erica Meg Parkinson and Laila Harbert were not released by their clubs to play.

Nevertheless, in 2022 and 2024, like the other home nations, they did not even qualify.

It is a far cry from the class of 2018 where the likes of Alessia Russo, Lauren Hemp and Georgia Stanway led the Lionesses to third place in the Under-20s World Cup, setting the tone for the incredible subsequent success.

Wiegman has handed debuts to 21 players since her arrival in September 2021, but only Lauren James, Hannah Hampton and Lucia Kendall have become established starters.

When England kick off in Crete on Friday, 5 October (20:00 BST), it is likely to be the same faces once again.

Young Lionesses win European trophy

To try and facilitate the pathway to top level football for young academy players, Football Association rules require WSL sides to include eight homegrown players in their squad lists.

The quota for WSL 2 clubs is higher and works on a sliding scale depending on squad size.

Former England striker Ellen White told the Women's Football Weekly podcast this was insufficient, saying: "We should be updating that quota of eight players, tweaking it to best help and complement our international structure, our homegrown talent."

"I would love to see them go much further - something mandated, a minimum on the pitch at any one time," the Guardian's Garry told BBC Women's Football Weekly. "London City's line-up was alarming.

"It's great for the product over here, but will we see pain in 15 years' time if England are struggling to go deep in major tournaments because we're not developing players?"

Last month, the FA approved a controversial plan to allow some WSL academy sides to play in the National League from 2027-28, saying it would "strengthen the women's football pyramid, raise standards across the league, and improve the development pathway for young players".

The FA believes this reform will address the relative lack of competitive minutes young English players receive.

Chelsea have already confirmed they plan to enter an academy side in the third tier and Manchester City women's managing director Charlotte O'Neill has previously said she would want to enter a team too.

title: Why is Monaco staging a sprint race? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
fullText:
Formula 1 has a rare Saturday race this weekend for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Kimi Antonelli goes into round 15 of the season with an imposing 81-point lead in the drivers' championship over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions before the event in Baku.

What are your thoughts on having a sprint race next year at Monaco? I was very surprised to see that on the calendar, given that the race has so little chance of overtaking - Graham

F1 to have 10 sprint races in 2027, including Monaco

Formula 1 announced the 2027 calendar last week, with the number of sprint events increased from six to 10, and one of them Monaco.

This has proved controversial with some fans.

Why pick the worst track on the calendar for overtaking to have two races in one weekend, some have wondered. What's the point of having two boring races; isn't one enough?

The thinking behind it, though, is less about the races than about qualifying, and how making Monaco a sprint could mix up the weekend.

Monaco qualifying is renowned as one of the highlights of the season. In that case, surely two great qualifying sessions is better than one?

It was also pointed out by F1 that it gives the chance of two different grid orders and therefore more variability.

There is another factor to consider, too.

Monaco is one of the most demanding tracks on the calendar, and it is renowned as somewhere drivers have to build up to the limit progressively so they can become confident with knowing how the car will behave when they get there.

Get that wrong, push too hard too soon, and the chances of an accident are considerably higher.

So asking the drivers to go straight into a qualifying after a single practice session is a really difficult challenge.

It is likely to mean more mistakes, more action, more drama, and therefore more entertainment.

The same goes for grand prix qualifying.

Yes, by then the drivers will have done a sprint race. But there are always changes made to the cars for qualifying, so again the drivers will be going in blind to some degree.

Yes, the sprint is likely to be a procession. How could it be anything else? But it adds an extra degree of jeopardy to the whole weekend.

Do you think F1 might consider the F2 approach for the virtual safety car, where drivers cannot pit under a VSC but can pit under a full safety car? As a regular viewer of both series, I think this works well in F2 and is another way to solve the jeopardy a short VSC period brings to a race. - Caroline

The VSC was discussed at the so-called FIA sporting advisory committee last week, but sources say no consensus emerged there as to potential changes.

It was also on the agenda for the F1 Commission meeting on Monday but there were no significant developments.

Lando Norris, who lost victory in Madrid by the VSC timing, said after the race that the drivers had previously discussed with the FIA the idea that the VSC should be out for a minimum of a lap so this sort of thing could not happen.

But every potential 'solution' comes with consequences. In that case, F1 might end up with a full lap of VSC just to recover a bit of debris.

The VSC was introduced so that relatively small-scale incidents could be dealt with without the lengthy disruption of a full safety car.

It's accepted that the safety car affords possibilities to gain and lose out, so why should the VSC not do the same? The argument is that, generally, these even out over the season, although the Norris case in Madrid had particularly dramatic consequences.

Antonelli benefited from this one, for example, but has lost out in other scenarios this year. For example, when the VSC gifted Lewis Hamilton the lead in Barcelona, even if that was rendered moot by Antonelli's subsequent retirement.

Why did Mercedes put George Russell on a two-stop strategy in the Spanish Grand Prix when the race has the longest pit lane of the season? George was the only driver out of the top 15 finishers on a two-stop and did this decision cost him a podium finish? - Richard

Mercedes were a bit stuck when the virtual safety car was deployed on lap 14 in Madrid.

The team had split the drivers' tyre strategies - Kimi Antonelli took the conventional strategy and started on the mediums, Russell had gone for the hards.

With overtaking so difficult in Madrid, it was always likely that one option would turn out to be sub-optimal. The timing of the VSC was very unfortunate for those who started on hard tyres because it coincided with the pit-stop window for those on mediums.

Mercedes had two choices - stay out, or pit and change tyre compound, as drivers are obligated to use two compounds during a dry grand prix.

Charles Leclerc, who also started on hards and was running immediately ahead of Russell, stayed out. Mercedes pitted in the hope of trying to beat Leclerc.

Whichever tyre Russell chose was unlikely to make it to the end, so Mercedes knew at that point they would almost certainly have to stop again.

The hard tyre was comfortably the best race tyre in Madrid, and on his mediums Russell did not have the pace to narrow the gap to Leclerc to less than it takes to do a pit stop. So there was nothing to lose by pitting again.

Team boss Toto Wolff said: "He said the tyres were not in a great shape, the mediums. We didn't think they would go to the end. (We thought) the better opportunity was not to hang out and wait for a red, but to change the tyres and get on with it."

Russell said: "Maybe I could have stayed out with Leclerc but I would have still finished behind him. Maybe I could have not pitted on to the hard again but everything I would have done would have brought us to the same position."

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Live and Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

During the Madrid race, Max Verstappen was told to hand the place back to Lewis Hamilton. Which he did. However, what would happen if Lewis had fallen maybe two or three cars further back. Does Max still have to hand back the place (and lose places to other cars) or would he just have to take a penalty? - Wayne

The scenario you paint actually happened in Madrid. Verstappen also got ahead of Antonelli on the first lap, so when Red Bull told him to let Hamilton by, he also had to let the Mercedes past.

Shortly after that happened, the message "no further action" was displayed on the timing screens and television coverage over the incident.

That was because Verstappen had given the place back by then. Otherwise, he would have been penalised.

So, yes, if a driver is adjudged to have committed an offence that requires giving the place back, they must do so regardless of whether there are at that point other cars between them.

There are two examples of this from Fernando Alonso's career.

In the 2005 Japanese Grand Prix, he passed Christian Klien's Red Bull by cutting the chicane, let him by again on the straight and then passed him into Turn One.

But race director Charlie Whiting did not notice that Alonso had let Klien back past, and after some discussions with the Renault team, he demanded Alonso cede the position.

That was two laps later, by which time Alonso was seven seconds up the road.

At Silverstone in 2010, Alonso, now at Ferrari, was forced off the track by Robert Kubica when trying an overtaking move at Vale, and ended up passing the Renault driver off the track.

Because he had been forced off, Ferrari decided not to give up the position. But Whiting told them they had to, after discussions with the team.

Problem was, at exactly that point, Kubica pulled into the pits to retire, so Alonso could not give the place back - and he was given a drive-through penalty.

Before he could serve it, there was then a safety-car period which closed up the field. Penalties could not be served under a safety car, so the two situations combined dropped Alonso right to the back of the field. He ended up finishing 14th, which was a costly blow to his title hopes.

title: Chelsea struggles to Villa bench - Garnacho faces defining season
description: Alejandro Garnacho joined Aston Villa on loan from Chelsea with a view to kick-starting his career, but his early weeks in the Midlands have been a struggle.
fullText:
Just like last season, questions are being asked about Alejandro Garnacho.

Two months after joining from Chelsea on an initial loan, the winger has yet to convince Aston Villa boss Unai Emery of his worth.

The Argentina forward has played just 31 minutes for Villa, spread across three substitute appearances.

A 15-minute outing against Hull is the most time he has spent on the pitch in a game.

Garnacho has been an unused substitute for Villa's past four matches , watching from the bench again as they won 3-2 at Tottenham on Saturday.

One goal and four assists in 24 Premier League games for Chelsea last term fell below what the Blues expected from their £40m recruit from Manchester United, so he was allowed to move on.

This campaign is only a month old, but 22-year-old Garnacho could be at a crossroads at Villa Park already.

Emery likes to ease new players into his teams.

Youri Tielemans did not start a Premier League game until November 2023 after joining in the summer, but became an integral part of Emery's machine.

Only Joao Gomes, out of 10 new summer signings, started Villa's opening Premier League game. Just two - Zion Suzuki and Nicolas Jackson - started the next.

Garnacho's situation feels extreme though, having been left on the bench for the Carabao Cup win at Coventry when Emery made seven changes.

Academy product George Hemmings, who joined Villa from Forest as a teenager, has started the season well to earn Emery's full trust and start ahead of Garnacho.

Ibrahim Mbaye, a £47m arrival from Paris St-Germain, made his first Villa start in the 3-1 victory at Coventry and is also preferred to Garnacho for now.

A facial injury in early August hampered Garnacho's pre-season and meant he missed the Super Cup defeat by Paris St-Germain, adding to the complications.

Emery needs his players to understand their roles and his methods before having full faith in them and he expects Garnacho to catch up.

"Continue working. Work, work, train, work," Emery said when asked about Garnacho's absence from the pitch.

"When he can have minutes to play, try to play well. He is progressing, but we have players in front of him now.

"George is playing fantastic. Alysson is also understanding things well and is giving us things I want. [Ibrahim] Mbaye also responded well.

"We want a competitive team and players to compete in the style we have. Garnacho is a little bit behind because of some circumstances we had in pre-season. It is time to be patient for the time he needs."

Garnacho, who first made his name as a livewire teenager, has shown in the past he can torment defences at Premier League level.

He spoke about needing time to adapt to a "different club and a different place" at Chelsea.

A further season of struggle would be a significant setback.

Emery is clearly yet to be convinced by what he sees in training, despite being a long-term Garnacho admirer.

Villa wanted more pace in their side and Crysencio Summerville was considered before he moved to Saudi Arabia's Al-Hilal.

Chelsea's £117m signing of Morgan Rogers from Villa left a gap for Emery to fill and Garnacho was available. A positive relationship between the clubs allowed for easy discussions.

Striker Jackson also joined from Chelsea for a Villa club record £65m and there have been eight deals between the clubs in the past four years.

Garnacho did not train with Xabi Alonso's Chelsea squad before leaving for Villa Park in July.

Roma were interested in the winger, but their loan offer did not suit Chelsea. Instead, Villa's deal gives the Blues the chance to make their money back after last year's outlay.

There is an obligation to buy tied into the loan that is believed to relate to appearances, and it is expected to be achievable - but that does not guarantee anything.

For instance, Harvey Elliott would have triggered a move worth £35m if he made just 10 Premier League appearances last season. As it turned out, the Liverpool loanee - now at Valencia - was used just four times by Villa in the top flight.

Emery did not feel the 23-year-old was good enough and made up his mind not to sign Elliott permanently just a couple of months into the season.

It raised the question for some within the game about whether a loan at Villa should be viewed with caution, and whether other players' careers could be derailed in the way Elliott experienced.

It was accepted that Elliott's options this summer were not as extensive following his season at Villa Park.

Time will tell whether Garnacho faces the same struggles, having experienced his career stalling over the past two years.

He made his Manchester United debut aged 17 and was part of Argentina's Copa America‑winning squad in 2024, but has not added to his eight international caps since November of that year.

The Madrid-born attacker also won the Premier League's goal of the season award in 2023-24 for his overhead kick against Everton while playing for United, but his output for Chelsea was disappointing.

Emery is waiting to see Garnacho fulfil his full potential at Villa, but the winger will have to wait until he gains the coach's trust, and then take his chance.

title: Pollock signs new Northampton deal in excess of £400K
description: Henry Pollock has brought an end to his contract stand-off with Northampton, saying it was ultimately "a very easy decision" to sign an extension.
fullText:
Henry Pollock has brought an end to his contract stand-off with Northampton, saying it was ultimately "a very easy decision" to sign an extension with the defending Prem champions.

"I am very, very happy to sign here," Pollock told BBC Radio Northampton.

"I have been here my whole career so it made sense for me to stay on the journey with such a young group of players, who are so ambitious.

"It was a very easy decision in the end."

The 21-year-old forward's new terms tie him to Northampton until the summer of 2028, raising the prospect of talks restarting in around a year's time.

Pollock, whose profile has exploded over the past two seasons after appearing for England and the British and Irish Lions, had been talked up as a "seven-figure player" during negotiations by his advisor Eddie Hearn.

However, the boxing promoter's valuation was never likely to be met at Northampton or elsewhere in the Prem, given Saints' star-studded line-up, the league's £6.4m squad salary cap and rules over players moving between clubs.

The exact level of Pollock's pay increase is unclear. While some sources have valued his new contract at £400,000 a year, others involved in the deal say the figure is higher.

His salary is certainly short of Scotland playmaker Finn Russell, who, as Bath's marquee player, is on the league's most lucrative package, worth about £1m a year.

Pollock's pay puts him well ahead of most of his contemporaries in the Prem, however.

His new deal is comfortably ahead of the average annual salary in the league (£191,000), the average earned by someone in his 20-22 age bracket (£106,000) and with his level of international experience (£224,000), as revealed by the latest league payroll data, covering the 2024-25 campaign., external

Only 4% of Prem players that season were paid in excess of £400,000 a year.

Pollock's previous contract, signed in December 2024, is understood to have been worth about £150,000.

"I don't create it, my team do," said Pollock of the speculation that has surrounded his future over the past seven weeks.

"It is one of those things that you have to take in your stride, but I am happy it is all done and I can focus on the rugby."

Asked about the possibility of Saints becoming the first side since Saracens in 2019 to successfully defend their English title, Pollock was bullish.

"We have the squad depth and the belief in this group that we can do it," he said.

"Let's see, hopefully we can create some magic along the way. Let's write a new story."

Pollock, who was instrumental in Northampton's run to the title last season, insisted last week that he was still open to offers, raising the possibility of a move abroad or even to another sport.

However, remaining at Northampton, for whom he made his league debut in November 2023, always seemed the most likely option.

After winning an age-grade world title with England's under-20s at the end of that season, Pollock returned to Franklin's Gardens and established himself as a first-team regular.

His pace, energy and on-pitch persona propelled him into the public consciousness and into contention for international honours.

He made his Test debut off the bench against Wales, scoring two tries, in March 2025 and was a bolter pick for the Lions squad only two months later.

His try-scoring feats through Saints' run to the Champions Cup final, complete with pre-planned celebrations, earned him a spot on the eight-strong shortlist for the continental competition's player of the year.

He has appeared in each of England's past 12 Tests, albeit with his only start coming in a 42-21 defeat by Ireland in February.

"Over the last few years, everyone has seen the quality he brings on the pitch and the speed of his rise through the game – but just as importantly, he's a young man of outstanding character," said Northampton's director of rugby Phil Dowson.

"What's most exciting is that there's still so much more to come from him. Henry is incredibly ambitious and constantly looking for ways to improve. He understands that individual success comes from contributing to a successful team, and he's already taken on leadership responsibilities within the squad despite his age.

"People sometimes underestimate how intelligent he is as a rugby player. When we sit down to review performances, he's often identified the same things we were going to discuss before we've even raised them. His understanding of the game is excellent, and that gives him a huge platform to keep progressing.

"He's become an important figure not just for Saints, but for the wider game. He inspires young supporters, brings excitement to rugby, and understands that everything off the pitch is built on performing consistently on it. We're excited to see what he can achieve over the coming years."

title: England fast bowler Wood retires from internationals
description: England fast bowler Mark Wood announces his retirement from international cricket with immediate effect.
fullText:
England fast bowler Mark Wood has announced his retirement from international cricket with immediate effect.

The 36-year-old, who is one of the fastest bowlers to ever play for England, has been blighted by injuries throughout his career.

The Durham paceman only returned to action in the first Ashes Test in Perth in November after 15 months out with an elbow injury followed by knee surgery.

However, he bowled just 11 overs before suffering swelling in the same left knee and subsequently flew home for treatment. He has not played for England since.

"Although this may not come as a surprise given the past year, it just feels like a natural time at the end of my contract," Wood said in a statement on social media.

"I've always tried to be resilient and come back from injury to prove people wrong and show everyone what I can do. Unfortunately, this time I lost the battle.

"On medical advice, Test cricket and 50-over cricket are not possible, so the England dream has slowly been ground out of me over the last year.

"Playing for England has been the greatest honour I could have ever wished for and a dream come true."

Wood added that he hopes to continue playing cricket in some capacity.

Wood took 119 wickets in 38 Tests after making his debut in 2015, and that summer he helped win back the Ashes on home soil.

However, he has suffered a string of ankle, knee and elbow injuries during his career.

In a bid to limit the stress on his body, he lengthened his run-up in 2018, and that did allow him to play key roles in some of England's biggest successes in recent years.

The altered run-up did not impact his pace and he was part of the team that lifted the 2019 50-over World Cup, where he took 18 wickets.

He was also in the squad that won the T20 World Cup in 2022, but missed the end stages of the tournament with a calf problem.

In white-ball cricket, Wood retires as England's sixth-highest wicket-taker in men's T20s with 54 from 38 matches, and he took 80 scalps in 70 one-day internationals.

Wood played a key role in helping England come from 2-0 down in the 2023 Ashes, with his return to the team - and blistering spells of bowling - helping them level the series.

"It's been a privilege to watch the latter part of a great career," said Rob Key, managing director of England men's cricket.

"To have been a point of difference in Ashes series wins, two World Cup wins, and to have thrilled crowds every time he got the ball in his hand is something very few players achieve. He can look back with enormous pride on a career very well spent."

Anyone who has ever played cricket at any level will have tried to bowl fast. The dream is to be able to hurtle the ball down at irresistible speed: batters flinching, stumps flying.

Mark Wood lived that dream. Few who have played for England, or any country, know what it is like to bowl with Wood's speed.

The sight of Wood flying in, bowling himself off his feet - literally, on many occasions - was one of the most thrilling in the game. He captured the imagination of supporters not only with his raw pace, but his personality. Wood engaged with supporters and never took himself too seriously. It seemed he always remembered that cricket is supposed to be fun.

Naturally, there will be the nagging doubt of what might have been had his career not been so badly hit by injuries. The human body is not designed to bowl fast and the rigours of the job hit Wood worse than most.

But, when the stars aligned, it was electrifying. A demolition of West Indies in St Lucia in 2019, complete with a remodelled, longer run-up, showed what Wood would be capable of in the latter part of his career.

He was one of the few England players to emerge with credit from the awful Ashes tour of 2021-22 and his entrance to the return series in 2023 was unforgettable.

Held back until the third Test, when England were already 2-0 down, Wood bowled at the speed of light at Headingley. In one of the great Ashes spells, Wood knocked over Usman Khawaja with a 95mph thunderbolt.

At the end of the Test, in a nail-biting run chase, Wood was at the crease with Chris Woakes to see England over the line. Woakes was another held back until the third Test and, without these great friends performing the way they did that summer, England would have been soundly beaten.

Wood has been a multi-format performer for England. He was in the XI on the unforgettable day at Lord's when the World Cup was won in 2019, coming out to bat with Ben Stokes despite carrying an injury. Wood was also in the squad when England lifted the T20 World Cup in 2022.

He is one of a handful of England players to have won both World Cups and the Ashes, having been part of the last England team to regain the urn in 2015. With Wood gone, the only remaining England player in Test cricket to have tasted Ashes glory is Joe Root.

There was no last hurrah in Australia. A long recovery from elbow and knee injuries did not produce the pace England were craving down under. Wood could only play in the first Test in Perth and said last month he was "ashamed" at what happened.

His retirement confirms the end of an era in English pace bowling. First Stuart Broad, then James Anderson, followed by Woakes and Wood into retirement. Throw in the all-round talent of Stokes, and England have lost 1,871 Test wickets in less than three years.

title: Man shot by ICE being detained with bullet still in his back, lawyer says
description:
A Venezuelan man who was shot by an immigration officer while delivering a DoorDash order in Austin, Texas, was transferred from the hospital to a detention center with a bullet still in his back, his lawyer said Monday.
Wilber Rafael Garces Perez was shot in the back by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer after the officer sideswiped the 28-year-old's car early Sunday afternoon, attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch told reporters at a Monday news conference. Garces Perez was then taken to the hospital, and his family was notified four hours later that he had been taken to the South Texas Processing Center in Pearsall, Texas, approximately a two-hour drive away from Austin, Lincoln-Goldfinch said. 
Garces Perez spoke by phone during the news conference, saying in Spanish that he was in a lot of pain. He explained that the bullet wasn't removed because it was lodged close to his spine.

title: 2 helicopter pilots killed while making water drops on Yosemite fire
description: The Dome fire burning in Yosemite national park on 15 September.Photograph: National Parks...
fullText:
Two helicopter pilots died while fighting a fire in Yosemite national park on Sunday afternoon.

The pilots were conducting water drops over the Dome fire, which had burned more than 3,000 acres since it ignited last week, when their helicopter crashed around 3pm, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.

The pilots were employed by the aerospace company Precision and were working with a wildland firefighting crew that specializes in using ropes to descend from helicopters to reach otherwise inaccessible terrain, known as helitack rappelling.

The helicopter went down southeast of Ostrander Lake, said Benjamin Cossel, a spokesperson with the Federal Complex Incident Management Team overseeing the firefighting response.

Details about the circumstances surrounding the crash were not immediately released. The crash will be investigated by the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board.

"It is with unimaginable sadness and broken hearts that we share the loss of two beloved members of our team," Precision wrote in a social media post. "We are devastated by this loss and are struggling to find the words. We ask for privacy and compassion for their families and our team as we grieve this tremendous loss."

The names of the pilots were not immediately released.

Roughly 580 people are fighting the Dome Fire, which started on 15 September near Wawona, California, according to the National Interagency Fire Center. It's burning on about 4.7 sq miles (12.3 sq km) and is about 15% contained. The lake near the crash site was roughly 9 miles (14.5km) south of Yosemite's iconic El Capitan, and about 7 miles (11.3km) northeast of Wawona.

Water-dropping helicopters have been key to fighting the blaze, which has spread across rugged terrain.

At least 14 people have died while helping with wildfires in the US this year, the most since 2022 when 25 deaths were recorded, according to government reports. Three firefighters died battling Colorado's Knowles fire, and an additional member of that crew succumbed to injuries weeks afterwards. The incident was the most deadly entrapment in 13 years.

The job has always carried inherent risks,but this year has been especially dangerous. The Trump administration has increased pressure on firefighting forces, amid a critical shortage of federal firefighters.

Gabrielle Canon contributed reporting

title: No criminal charges in death of Mississippi teen Nolan Wells, grand jury finds
description:

The report says that the "position of, condition of, time of discovery, and location" of the 18-year-old's body off the coast of Mississippi this July is "consistent with drowning."
Wells vanished after he and friends had gone out celebrating the Fourth of July holiday on barrier islands off the Gulf Coast. His body was recovered in the waters off Horn Island two days later.
Authorities have previously said they believe the college football player drowned, but the final determination would go to a grand jury that would review all the case materials, including the state medical examiner's completed autopsy report, to decide whether Wells' death involved a crime.
fullText:
Wells vanished after he and friends celebrated July 4 off the Gulf Coast.

The grand jury reviewing the evidence in the death of Nolan Wells has found that no criminal charges are warranted at this point, according to the Jackson County Grand Jury Report released late Monday night.

The report says that the "position of, condition of, time of discovery, and location" of the 18-year-old's body off the coast of Mississippi this July is "consistent with drowning."

Wells vanished after he and friends had gone out celebrating the Fourth of July holiday on barrier islands off the Gulf Coast. His body was recovered in the waters off Horn Island two days later.

Authorities have previously said they believe the college football player drowned, but the final determination would go to a grand jury that would review all the case materials, including the state medical examiner's completed autopsy report, to decide whether Wells' death involved a crime.

The grand jury of 23 people, convened last week, found "no credible evidence to support the public allegations" that anyone riding to or from the island that day surrounding Wells "engaged in any criminal conduct related to" his death.

The panel was comprised of what the report called a "cross section of citizens" from the area: 13 men and ten women, including "12 Caucasians, five African Americans, one Asian, two Hispanics, two Native Americans, and one individual who preferred 'other.'" Their ages ranged from 27 years old to 68 years old.

The grand jury heard from 43 witnesses and reviewed materials including physical evidence collected at the scene, digital evidence, police reports and interviews, videos, images and maps collected during the investigation.

That Wells drowned is a conclusion by the process of elimination, the grand jury report said, adding that the condition of the body made it harder to figure out. The long-awaited toxicology report was "not particularly informative as decomposition fluid is an unreliable source for evaluating substance levels within a body."

The panel found, however, that Wells had no cocaine in his system and no evidence he'd ever used it. The panel did find that Wells bought alcohol with a fake ID, and no adults of alcohol-buying age provided any to him on the island that day.

There was bruising on the back of Wells' head, which was "not a fatal injury," the report said. The grand jury "found no evidence of any fatal injury or organic disease to Mr. Wells' body."

The report said it's still unclear how Wells got that bruise on his head.

One witness testified under oath that around the time of his last being seen, they saw Wells "slip awkwardly off the side of a boat" but "could not say whether Mr. Wells struck his head during the fall," and that he "continued to socialize after the fall and did not appear injured."

"The Grand Jury finds that Mr. Wells was not in any physical altercation or argument on July 4, 2026," the report said.

Much of the report also addresses the sudden deluge of national attention in the wake of Wells' death, as well as the online speculation and even interstate threats the pending investigation has garnered.

Addressing unanswered questions about Wells' phone, which was retrieved later from friends on the mainland after he went missing, the report said the panel found "it is not unusual or suspicious for individuals to return from the island on boats they did not travel to the island on; nor is it unusual for individuals to place their phones and personal items on other boats they visit and socialize on.

The Grand Jury finds that Mr. Wells' phone was not the only phone to travel back to the mainland without its owner."

The "public clamor and malicious allegations against the occupants of" the three boats on which Wells and his friends went to the island "have extended to their family members and friends," and that the "public attacks" are "malicious, false, and have no truth in fact or evidence," the report said.

The report said Wells' family was given the opportunity to produce evidence from their private investigation into Wells' death and the family's lawyers advised that their investigation "revealed no witnesses or evidence whom the legal team reasonably believes possess information germane to potential criminal activity that warrants referral."

The report also noted that there is no statute of limitations on homicide cases in the State of Mississippi. "If credible evidence comes to light in the future that suggests Mr. Wells' death was non-accidental, this matter should be represented to the Jackson County Grand Jury for further consideration," the report said.

description:

US President Donald Trump is expected to claim he is winning both on the battlefield and as a peacemaker Tuesday in a speech to the United Nations overshadowed by growing spillover from his stalled war against Iran.
Trump will likely not hold back in renewing his frequent boasts that under him the United States is "the hottest country" in the world.
