fullText:
US President Donald Trump is expected to claim he is winning both on the battlefield and as a peacemaker Tuesday in a speech to the United Nations overshadowed by growing spillover from his stalled war against Iran.

Trump will likely not hold back in renewing his frequent boasts that under him the United States is "the hottest country" in the world.

He is also expected to seek to justify the Iran war, which has so far failed to fulfil White House objectives and provoked widespread economic damage over the Strait of Hormuz's closure.

But the self-styled peacemaker could equally use the UN stage to tout his controversial efforts to end the Gaza conflict and his ongoing effort to bring more Arab countries into the Abraham Accords with Israel.

"No one knows what Trump is going to say, not even Trump's speechwriters," International Crisis Group's Daniel Forti said.

"This year, we expect more of a contrast between Trump, sort of both announcing and celebrating his record as a peacemaker versus defending his ongoing military operations around the world," said Forti.

"It's not entirely clear what reaction Trump's going to get from world leaders."

The keynote speech at the start of the UN General Assembly High-level week will provide Trump with a big platform to renew his frequent assaults on the global body.

Last year's speech was characterized by Trump's extraordinary accusations of UN sabotage when an escalator in the New York headquarters briefly stopped working and the teleprompter glitched.

Trump has regularly attacked the UN and its leader Antonio Guterres since returning to office, although Washington last week reportedly paid $725 million into its budget, avoiding the embarrassment of losing some of its voting rights.

He is also likely to meet skepticism over his claims of a historic win for the United States when a security deal is signed Tuesday for a US presence in Greenland -- a territory of Denmark that Trump repeatedly threatened, driving bitter divisions through longtime US-led alliances.

As well as his closely watched speech to the General Assembly, Trump will hold side meetings with Britain's new prime minister, Andy Burnham, as well as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, Japanese premier Sanae Takaichi and Venezuela's interim leader Delcy Rodriguez.

Rodriguez has governed under intense American pressure since her predecessor Nicolas Maduro was captured by US forces in January.

Last year, Trump's speech to the gathering of world leaders veered into a rant about an escalator that stalled as he was using it, suggesting it was done deliberately.

He also railed against a defective teleprompter, falsely accused London's mayor of imposing Islamic law and said Europe was in "serious trouble" over migration.

Trump clearly has not gotten over the incidents.

"They turned off the escalator," Trump said last week in the Oval Office.

"Fortunately, my first lady was very strong and I was able to grab her back or another part of her body. It was actually a little bit lower than the back," he said.

The offending escalator "has been checked and rechecked," Guterres's spokesman Stephane Dujarric said Monday.

"New arrangements were made to facilitate the US delegation's use of a teleprompter, they now have a separate booth, so we hope that will work without a hitch," he added.

Guterres, who kicks off the week of speeches, is expected to touch on the explosion of artificial intelligence and the multiple wars raging globally.

Next up -- just before Trump -- will be Brazilian President Lula Inacio Lula da Silva, whose country by tradition is always first to speak at the annual gathering of leaders.

Trump, who has supported Lula's opponents and other right-wing candidates across Latin America, may not like what he hears.

Leftist Lula, running for reelection, said last week that he would tell Trump to not "meddle" in Brazil's upcoming vote.

Protesters against Missouri's congressional redistricting plan gather outside the Missouri Capitol in Jefferson City on May 12. - David A. Lieb/AP/File
A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election but put that ruling on hold for a week so the Supreme Court could review the dispute.

fullText:
A federal appeals court ruled Monday that Missouri must use a GOP-friendly congressional redistricting plan for November’s election but put that ruling on hold for a week so the Supreme Court could review the dispute.

The ruling from the US 8th Circuit Court of Appeals is the latest twist in a whiplash legal wrangling over the map of the state’s eight congressional districts, injecting another round of uncertainty, as it does not take effect immediately but rather sets up another round of appeals.

The Missouri Supreme Court previously said the 7-1 Republican-leaning map adopted by the legislature last year could not be used because of a referendum challenge brought against it under the state constitution. Instead, the court ordered election officials to use an older, 6-2 redistricting plan even though the 2025 plan had been used in the state’s primary. The US Supreme Court declined to reverse that ruling, and it then paused a federal judge’s ruling that sought to revive the 7-1 map.

The new ruling from the 8th Circuit said requiring voters to cast general election ballots on the older plan violates the US Constitution.

It relied on estimates put forward by a conservative group in the case to conclude “that more than 1.4 million Missourians could not vote for the congressional district nominees who will appear on their November 2026 general election ballot, and more than a quarter-million Missourians who voted in the August 2026 primary election cast a vote for a congressional district candidate who now cannot represent them.”

Missouri’s new map targeted the 5th Congressional District, held by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, by breaking up its Kansas City base and stretching it into rural and Republican-leaning parts of the state.

The group that launched the referendum campaign against the GOP-leaning map noted in a statement reacting to the new ruling that “Ballots have been printed, and Missourians have already voted.”

“Thousands more will vote before this order seeks to take effect,” the statement from People Not Politicians said. “Officials should stop wasting taxpayers’ money on pointless legal action and instead focus on administering our elections.”

This story has been updated to correctly reflect the number of congressional districts in Missouri.

CNN’s Fredreka Schouten and John Fritze contributed to this report.

description: The Rams are playing without wide receiver Puka Nacua and pass rusher Myles Garrett.
fullText:
The Rams are playing without wide receiver Puka Nacua and pass rusher Myles Garrett. They haven't missed them so far tonight, with the Giants having lost quarterback Jaxson Dart on the first possession.

Stafford has thrown for 184 yards and two touchdowns, with Davante Adams catching five for 145 and a touchdown.

Rams defensive lineman Aaron Donald has three tackles, including one for loss, in his first game action in 981 days. Donald retired after the 2023 season but officially unretired Aug. 30.

Adams, 31, has not had a better game since Dec. 15, 2024, against the Jaguars when he caught nine passes for 198 yards and two touchdowns.

Stafford has completed 11 of 15 passes and has thrown a pick. His touchdowns covered 31 yards to Adams and 10 yards to running back Kyren Williams.

The Rams should have had three more points to end the half, but kicker Harrison Mevis missed a 43-yard try wide left on the final play of the half.

Giants safety Jevon Holland has done everything he can to keep his team in it. Holland, who had an interception of Dak Prescott last week, has an interception, a forced fumble and a recovered fumble.

At the end of a 5-yard Kyren Williams run late in the first half, Holland punched the ball out and recovered it at the Los Angeles 11. It was Williams' eighth career fumble.

The Giants had six possessions in the first half and four times crossed midfield with drives to the Los Angeles 43, 43, 18 and 3 without a touchdown. After Holland's fumble recovery, the Giants settled for Dominic Zvada's chip-shot, 24-yard field goal with 25 seconds left in the half.

Dart went 3-of-5 for 20 yards before injuring his left knee. Jameis Winston replaced him and was 4-of-12 for 58 yards and an interception, a throw straight to Rams cornerback Trent McDuffie in the end zone.

Cam Skattebo has only 18 yards on seven carries.

title: Jaxson Dart injury: Everything we know as Giants’ QB leaves game vs. Rams
description: We will keep you posted as information becomes available.
fullText:
New York Giants quarterback Jaxson Dart went down with what appeared to be a left knee injury on the team's first drive Monday night against the Los Angeles Rams.

Dart was sandwiched between Rams defenders Byron Young and Josaiah Stewer on a third-and-8 incompletion to Theo Johnson from the Rams' 41-yard line.

Dart did walk slowly off the field under his own power. Dart has been ruled out. GM Joe Schoen told ESPN that the quarterback is "going to be OK."

Jameis Winston took over at quarterback for the Giants on their second offensive series.

Dart protecting himself from big hits and concussions has been a constant story. This, though, was a hit from the pocket after which his left knee appeared to bend in an awkward manner.

Dart limped slowly to the locker room after being checked in the medical tent.

John Harbaugh had this to say about Dart's injury during a brief halftime interview:

"We're just focused on the second half, trying to find a way to win the game. We're not thinking about that right now."

Dr. David Chao, a former NFL team doctor who goes by @ProFootballDoc on X, offered a quick take on the injury.

Not expecting season ending
Hard to return but not surgical injury
Foot off the ground saves him🙏 https://t.co/qXROCLhts9

Good news for Jaxson Dart: By video, I do not believe he suffered a season-ending ACL tear.

The concern is an MCL sprain, an injury likely measured in weeks, not months. The MRI will determine the severity. pic.twitter.com/6uS1bteswL

Several starting quarterbacks have already suffered injuries this season. That list includes Sam Darnold of the Seattle Seahawks, Jayden Daniels of the Washington Commanders, and Caleb Williams of the Chicago Bears.

We will have more on Dart's injury when it becomes available.

title: Why Jayson Tatum Drastically Makes Celtics Numerically Scary NBA Title Contenders
description: Jayson Tatum will have a bigger role with the Celtics for the 2026-27 NBA season. We break down whether that's good or bad for Brad Stevens and Joe Mazzulla. after the Jaylen Brown trade for Paul George
fullText:
Why Jayson Tatum Drastically Makes Celtics Numerically Scary NBA Title Contenders originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

All eyes are on Jayson Tatum. It has become clear, especially after the Jaylen Brown trade, that this is his team now. Coach Joe Mazzulla has built schemes and rotations to win with the nine-year veteran as their primary superstar. For now, it may be counterintuitive to think the Boston Celtics are contenders after parting ways with an NBA MVP candidate and former NBA Finals MVP. But it will all make sense by the end of this article. We will even tackle how Brad Stevens, Paul George, Hugo Gonzalez, and Mitchell Robinson fit into this.

For the outsider looking in, or even just the common NBA fan, it's hard to understand why the Celtics are contenders after having just dealt Jaylen Brown for Paul George. But the best way to make sense of things is to step into the mind of Coach Joe Mazzulla and Brad Stevens. What language do they speak and thrive in? Numbers. Do not be intimidated because we will make all of the graphs and numbers digestible for every fan to enjoy.

Before diving deep into how Jayson Tatum impacts the Celtics, there needs to be an understanding of the system that this team has run for the past few years, which led them to the 2024 NBA Championship. An offense that tanks pace to become the most efficient version of themselves. Even with Jrue Holiday, Kristaps Porzingis, Al Horford, and Jaylen Brown on the team, this overarching philosophy was already in place.

Let's look at how Coach Joe Mazzulla and the Celtics did offensively in 2025-26, then move from there.

(Numbers scraped from Basketball Reference)

A few notable raw numbers pop out here. The Celtics are the best team in ball security, with a league-leading 0.112 TOV% (turnover percentage), and they're also a potent offense, as shown by a 120.8 ORTG (offensive rating) that ranks second in the NBA. Coach Mazzulla has also schemed them to get second-chance points and extra possessions, as shown by the league's sixth-best ORB% at 0.292.

However, it is weird that the Celtics have the seventh-best FT% (free throw percentage) at 0.807, but they are 29th in their free throw rate at just 0.167. There are answers for why that's the case, and it all has to do with Tatum only playing 16 games during the 2025-26 NBA season.

Prior to getting to that point, the offensive landscape of the Celtics during the 2025-26 NBA season, when broken down into the gradient vectors of eFG%, TOV%, ORB%, and FTR, then compared to the rest of the NBA, looks like this.

More: Jayson Tatum gets honest about how he feels about LeBron James joining the 76ers

Let's slowly discuss what these mean.

For starters, the Celtics, through Coach Mazzulla's schemes, run a very efficient offense when scaled to the rest of the NBA. Where does it say that? Well, they have a 55.3% eFG%, which is above the league average of 54.67%. But that's not the sole metric for efficiency; anyone who claims that would be lying to NBA fans. It is also supplemented by Boston's 29.27% ORB%, which ranked sixth in the NBA and is far higher than the league average of 26%. So, a large semblance of offensive efficiency is on their side.

Second, this is where things get a bit more technical, but do not fret. When analyzing the chart, the Celtics have a sensitivity of 1.899 to the league average of 1.785. Similarly, they have a maximum slope of 1.3, while the NBA average is 1.19. It sounds like a word salad right now, but we'll make it simpler.

See, the Celtics run the slowest offense in the NBA. They have a pace of 94.8, dead last in the league. This means that possessions matter more. Personally, I like to call it the Mazzulla or Love and Trust Sensitivity. Coach Mazzulla's offensive system uses more of the 24-second shot clock than the other 29 teams, runs plays perfectly rather than chucking up haphazard shots, and has everyone try to find the best shot possible as the offense moves.

The sequence typically goes: Derrick White or Payton Pritchard slowly brings the ball up, they signal the play to be run, constant passes are thrown while others like Neemias Queta or Jordan Walsh move off-ball through cuts to secure an offensive rebound, and then someone takes the highest-value shot. What's the ideal outcome? The Celtics either sink the field goal or get a rebound. Notice, the other option of getting a foul to take free throws a la Luka Doncic, Giannis Antetokounmpo, or Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is not an option here. All of this explains why the Celtics have a high sensitivity and are volatile to 'getting in their own way'. Fewer possessions and pace mean more pressure to knock down shots while milking the clock.

🍀Boston Celtics 2025-2026 ~ Flare screen plays + Variations

- Flare screen = off-ball screen between passer and recipient

Variations include :
-> Early offense Flares
-> Chest (Horns/Ram/Spain/Zoom/Zipper/Stagger)
-> Flip Flare
-> Zoom Flare
-> Veer Flare pic.twitter.com/TR2vrjhfed

Third, when the Celtics execute Coach Mazzulla's schemes well, they lock down the half-court and limit opponents' chances to beat them in transition. With a high 0.553 eFG%, they miss less and force opponents into fewer defensive rebounds. Boston also has a high 0.292 ORB%, which beats most squads in turning their own misses into second-chance points and extra possessions. Adding their league-leading 0.112 TOV% to their fairly high eFG% means offensive possessions either end on a high-quality shot or a reset shot clock. In both scenarios, they can set up a better shot or execute defensive schemes more cleanly, given the time to get back on the other side of the court.

This is what the Mazzulla Sensitivity and Tank-Pace-For-Efficiency schemes do for the Celtics.

So, where does Jayson Tatum fit into these?

More: Jayson Tatum puts the false narratives to rest regarding his friendship with Jaylen Brown

The easiest way to understand Coach Joe Mazzulla and Brad Stevens' situation with their new star is that it is not complex at all. Jayson Tatum is the Celtics' offensive insurance card, but he comes with a steep upfront tax. No, this isn't about him being an Amica Insurance ambassador, nor is it about his five-year, $313.9 million deal. It's about how the Celtics change when they have their superstar on the court.

To make more sense of this, let's look deeper into his numbers during the 2025-26 NBA season.

A few notes before breaking this further down. Tatum's 49.3 eFG% is the lowest he recorded in the past six seasons. The same goes for his 41.1% FG%; it is the lowest of his career.

Now, it's easier to visualize why Tatum has a steep cost when the Celtics run their offense through him. Diving deeper into the data, the Celtics take a hit in major categories. They get a -7.5 ORTG, and their eFG% goes down to -0.6 back in the 2025-26 season. But this isn't a sign of concern. See, he had only just returned from an Achilles injury, and the recovery took less than a year. He had to shift his weight so the injury wouldn't reaggravate. This is reflected in career lows in his 49.3% eFG% and 41.1% FG%.

Another major factor is Coach Mazzulla and the Celtics giving Tatum the green light to run their plays in isolation. Remember the ideal sequence to balance out the Mazzulla Sensitivity? Well, a large chunk of that gets thrown away when someone plays isolation ball. Jaylen Brown also saw this happen when he led the Celtics without Tatum. The star milks the shot clock in isolation, which drags down their ORTG and eFG%. For a team that plays at a low pace like the Celtics, the numbers drop significantly when they play in isolation because extra possessions are rarely available.

Coach Mazzulla's system also takes a drastic plunge in ORB% when Tatum is on the floor if he plays in isolation. It goes down by -0.275. Why is that the case? See, isolation drives in the Celtics system usually mean someone unleashes their 'bag work,' and the remaining four players have to move closer to the perimeter to clear the lane for a drive or a kickout three-pointer. This turns off a high ORB%. However, he does have the playmaking chops to avoid all of these woes.

Jayson Tatum 25 PTS, 18 REB, 11 AST at Miami (2026) pic.twitter.com/huOQr3FWKZ

This is where the new additions and Brad Stevens' hesitance to let go of a certain player comes in. The Mitchell Robinson acquisition solves the ORB% problem because he led the NBA with his 23.1% ORB%. Paul George solves the other part of it: bail-out corner three-pointers or a secondary immediate playmaker. The player traded for Brown recorded the fourth-best eFG%  in his career, valued at 53.6%. Hugo Gonzalez? He's the perfect Swiss Army knife able to patch all of these deficiencies when isolation ball is played. The Celtics rookie had a 56.1% eFG% that bailed them out late in the shot clock and a 6.4% ORB%, which is exceptionally high for a small forward. He is on par with guys like Josh Hart and Keldon Johnson in the rebounding category despite being 6'6".

Tatum will thrive with these new acquisitions.

More: Paul George gets real about how he views Jayson Tatum as the only superstar in Boston

Last, and definitely not least, all of this is worth it because Tatum thrives in either team-executed schemes or isolation. The Celtics star improves their ball security as the primary ball handler. Coach Mazzulla can breathe a sigh of relief because he knows the Celtics won't commit turnovers when the superstar has the ball. More importantly, the option for free throw attempts that were not afforded to them when Jaylen Brown ran the offense- remember that? That's the biggest pull Tatum has, and it makes them more lethal. He opens up the offense by giving them second chances to score at the free-throw line because his ability to draw fouls is impeccable. The Celtics have a +0.108 higher free-throw rate and a +0.016 higher free-throw percentage. Coupling that with a low turnover percentage and high offensive rebounding rate means they have all that it takes to win the NBA championship for the 2026-27 season.

What about the deficiencies? Well, Tatum has a whole offseason to address his injuries and shot mechanics. Basketball-Reference projects his field goal percentage rising from 41.1% to 44.7%, while his three-point percentage rises from 32.9% to 34.6%. All of these will keep Mazzulla's sensitivity in check.

Yes, the Philadelphia 76ers now have Jaylen Brown and LeBron James. The Miami Heat will see Giannis Antetokounmpo, while the Indiana Pacers get Tyrese Haliburton back. But the Celtics have gotten scarier. Why? It's because they are set to be more stable, unlike in previous years when two people played isolation. With Tatum back in the rotation and new additions to make their Mazzulla Sensitivity more manageable, it looks like a dark horse in the Eastern Conference will go unnoticed as they retain the top spot.

title: US threatens to ground Iranian airlines worldwide from Wednesday
description: Treasury Secretary says airports and companies servicing Iranian carriers risk being cut off from the US dollar system.
fullText:
United States Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent says Iranian airlines could effectively be shut out of international travel from Wednesday, as Washington threatens foreign companies with secondary sanctions if they continue servicing the country’s carriers.

“On September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world,” Bessent told CNBC on Monday.

The warning is aimed not just at the airlines themselves, but at the airports, fuel suppliers, ticketing companies and other businesses they rely on to operate abroad.

“If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets, or you will be knocked out of the dollar system,” Bessent said.

The threat marks the latest step in US President Donald Trump administration’s escalating economic campaign against Tehran, which has continued alongside the war between the US and Iran.

Earlier this month, the US Treasury imposed sanctions on all remaining Iranian airlines that had not already been targeted, as well as companies outside Iran accused of supporting the country’s aviation sector.

Iran’s aviation industry was already heavily constrained by years of US sanctions, which have made it difficult for carriers to buy new aircraft and obtain spare parts and maintenance services.

The measures are part of a much broader sanctions regime aimed at isolating Iran from the international financial system. US secondary sanctions threaten foreign companies that do business with Iran across sectors including energy, shipping, technology, gold and digital assets with penalties of their own.

Bessent’s comments came a day after talks with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, ahead of Trump’s meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

China is one of Iran’s most important economic partners and diplomatic backers, making Beijing’s cooperation potentially significant to Washington’s efforts to financially isolate Tehran.

Bessent said Chinese officials had been “very engaged” in the US pressure campaign. Washington was holding what he described as positive talks with Chinese financial authorities, including People’s Bank of China Governor Pan Gongsheng, about compliance with US sanctions on Iran.

Muse exposes an undocumented setting:

endo_voyager_dictation_endpoint

A local attacker or malware can modify this endpoint without special privileges.

Once redirected, dictated prompts can be sent to an attacker-controlled endpoint, potentially allowing:

In short: Muse’s access can potentially become the attacker’s access.

The PoC implements a subset of the 50+ commands exposed by Muse.

Once running, click the microphone button in Muse and dictate a prompt to trigger the PoC.

This is a local attack. An attacker must already be able to execute code as the local user.

The concern is that Muse may have significantly broader access than ordinary local malware, making it a particularly useful target for privilege/access amplification.

title: I built an autonomous accounting tool to let AI do my taxes
description: Self-hosted bookkeeping for a small Canadian corporation: receipts and bank statements in, a reconciled, audit-ready ledger out. Bring your own vision LLM. AGPL-3.0, no telemetry. - CodeGameDev29/K...
fullText:
Watch the demo  ·  Quickstart  ·  How it works  ·  Your data  ·  Known issues

Autonomous Accounting turns a pile of receipts, invoices and bank statements into a
reconciled, categorized ledger — plus an audit binder with every source document
attached. A vision LLM you choose reads the documents, a four-pass matcher pairs them with
your bank lines, and anything it is not sure of is flagged for you instead of guessed.
Everything runs on one machine you own: no account to create, no vendor to pay, no copy of
your books anywhere but your own disk.

Two minutes twenty: one invented company's January, from eight documents and a bank CSV to a
downloadable audit binder.

Watch the full demo (2:20, captioned, no sound)

Everything shown is synthetic. python scripts/gen_demo_data.py writes the same month on
your machine — see Try the demo month.

The long form — backups, encryption at rest, what reaches a model — is in
Honesty about data.

You need Python 3.11+, Node 20+, PostgreSQL 15+ on loopback, and any
OpenAI-compatible, vision-capable endpoint — vLLM, llama.cpp, Ollama's /v1, LM Studio.
This project hosts no model of its own.

Registration is closed by default. Set AUTH_ALLOW_SIGNUP=1, restart, sign up, then set it
back to 0. GET /health reports database, storage and LLM reachability.

Generate each secret exactly as .env.example says:

and set DATABASE_URL to the database you are about to create. Every other variable, with
its default, is in .env.example. AUTH_AUTOCONFIRM=1 (the default) means a new account
works immediately without any mail transport.

local_auth_schema.sql must run first: it creates the auth schema, auth.uid() and the
authenticated role, all of which schema_pg.sql needs. schema_pg.sql is the whole
schema — every table, index, trigger and row-level-security policy — as a single baseline;
db/migrations/ ships empty and python -m db.migrate therefore has nothing to do on a
fresh install, but run it anyway so anything added after the baseline is picked up.
local_grants.sql must run last: it grants on the tables the steps above created, and
without it every query fails with permission denied. Each step is idempotent, so
re-running the sequence on an existing database changes nothing. (Nothing in db/ needs a
server feature newer than PostgreSQL 13; 15 is just the oldest release still maintained
upstream.)

FastAPI serves the built bundle from the same origin. For frontend work, run the Vite dev
server instead, which proxies /api to the backend:

The reasonableness engine needs a benchmark table, which is not committed:

That downloads the Financial Performance Data CSVs published by Innovation, Science and
Economic Development Canada on the Government of Canada Open Government Portal, normalises
them into per-industry cohort cells, validates them fail-loud, and writes a large JSON file
that .gitignore excludes. The data is licensed under the Open Government Licence –
Canada; the generated file and every report built from it carry the attribution the
licence requires. No Open Government Licence data file is distributed with this repository
— you build the table yourself. See NOTICE.

Every run validates structure and plausibility. --anchor anchor.json adds an optional
check that one named cell still carries the figures you expect, so a refresh that quietly
changes what a cell means aborts instead of overwriting your table; with no anchor
supplied, no cell-specific figures are demanded.

--seed-only writes a small table of invented example figures instead, with no download —
enough for the engine and its tests to run, and labelled in its own meta as not being
industry data. Skip the step entirely and the feature stays off; nothing else is affected.

The files under tests/fixtures/ are per-parser unit fixtures; uploaded through the UI they
match nothing, because no receipt among them belongs to any bank line. To see the whole
pipeline work, generate a coherent synthetic month instead:

That writes one invented company's January 2026 — a 12-row CAD statement in the built-in
CSV layout, seven PDFs and one PNG — plus a README.txt saying what each file is there to
show. Then, in the app:

What that run looks like on one model is written up under Verification gaps in
docs/backlog.md, next to the defects it found.

One thing a stranger will meet early: Gmail's OAuth redirect has to match what you
registered. The code builds <BASE_URL>/api/onboarding/gmail/callback, and BASE_URL
defaults to http://localhost:8080. If you serve the app anywhere else, set BASE_URL (or
GMAIL_REDIRECT_URI) before connecting Gmail, and register the same value with Google.
Gmail, PayPal and Wise gather integrations stay hidden until you configure credentials.

See CONTRIBUTING.md: synthetic fixtures only, ruff and tsc clean, one
topic per pull request, sign off your commits (git commit -s). The most useful
contribution is a statement parser or a category rule for a layout the engine does not read
yet — built from invented data, never real books.

If this saved you a bookkeeping afternoon, a star helps the next small-business owner find it.

title: We're Using AI Wrong. The Chat Window Sucks
description: Why a persistent document with a threaded comment rail beats a chat thread for real work with an agent, and the pace it made possible on one site build.
fullText:
AI chat windows are everflowing rivers where every leaf you drop into that river immediately floats away, and good luck finding it. Type something, the agent responds, and within seconds the answer scrolls up and out of sight.

How often do you go hunting through your endlessly scrolling chat to try and find something that was said just a minute ago? It's almost like we WANT it to look like the Matrix. Never has a good designer said "Let's show the user all the different function calls the backend is making to show this webpage," but that's what a chat window does. It's a terrible UX.

Markdown (.md) documents are cool, but they came and went faster than we let our Tamagotchis die in the 90s. Now, HTML as an everyday document is the new sliced bread (yes, thank you Boris).

HTML docs were initially great because they are beautiful and easier to read, but also more functional. First we remembered that HTML allows live elements like interactive graphs. And holy-fricking-cow that's so much cooler than a .doc or .ppt.

But local HTML-as-a-document has a secret: you can turn any local HTML page into an interface for your AI.

I'm not the first or only person to have done this. It's a logical next step. A lot of people are figuring it out at the same time because the existing conditions make it only one step away from where we're standing.

The pain is simple and pervasive: I don't want to copy/paste things back and forth from a chat window to a document. And I want to be able to find what we said when we were workshopping that title without scrolling the endless chat.

When HTML lives on your machine, it's really easy to inject additional functionality into it. By combining a locally running server with an injected javascript package, you can create a direct interface to your AI, in your browser. This is Lahe, the Live Agentic HTML Editor, a quality of life tool that I built largely to make my own processes better.

Once we create this pattern, suddenly a whole host of fun new ways of working opens up.

First, I don't actually want that sidebar visible most of the time. Collapse it, get rid of it, and now I'm looking at a document that looks like a webpage, but I can select anything and edit it.

When building this website, I spent a lot of time creating a style system. This simple-bordering-on-boring set of fonts, colors, and layouts is the result of over 700 comments and edits over the course of two days. Using this document review tool Claude and I iterated over 97 different review pages, 49 different logo options, examined over 85 stock images from Pexels, created 19 original line drawings and 17 original video files

At that clip, the act of just having to switch windows to the chat is enough to significantly hamper the velocity.

The design process I followed actually used over 120 subagents. And you start to realize, well if I've got a bunch of subagents at my disposal from the browser, can't I do a lot more than edit this document?

Yes. Yes you can. Now your todo list (or "daily briefing" or whatever fun name you're calling it), can create a line item that says "Don't forget you need to email your weekly report" and you can click that item and say "draft that up for me please."

Without ever leaving your todo list. And if you want to take it a step further, well you own the todo list format, so why not just add a button that will trigger the AI to go off and take care of it without you having to say anything at all? With HTML as the medium we have the last 20 years of UX learnings as options for how to interact with AI.

This small change, not having to leave your todo list, is great for reducing task switching. And when you're as ADHD as I am, it keeps you from wandering off on 17 tangents because you opened your email.

It turns out you can also have one agent managing multiple tabs.

While working on this article I said, from within the page, "Help me workshop the title. I want good hooks," and Claude opened another tab for me, where we went through 3 rounds of "more of this, less of that" and finally arrived at a title.

And because it’s so easy, the bandwidth of information between myself and the agent is increasing. So I am giving more and more information about what I want and like, which means I'll get better results from the AI.

At that point I told the second tab, "Ok we found it. Plug this in to the article." I closed the tab and went back to the article, and the title updated on the original tab.

That should feel a little mind-blowing. Tabs open for me automatically when I need a new surface to workshop something, and when we're done and I close them, the final result is automatically plugged back in to the core working document.

From here the next level is to talk. Use your words. Out loud. If you're not using a voice transcription service yet, it's incredible.

As someone who is very adhd and very physically-oriented, I have long dreamt of being able to pace around the room while getting work done, but I've always been chained to my keyboard. (There's certainly some satisfaction in good, accurate, fast typing though too).

Add voice transcription and you can walk around your office, microphone in hand, rattling off your outline to an AI that can assemble a structure for you to fill in.

Since Lahe is working in HTML, we can now use this editing style for documents, presentations, and even our webpage designs.

When I review new features now, I can comment directly in the HTML as I walk through the feature. Again it's an ostensibly small change, but the impact is pretty great.

I do enjoy writing, but I also don't need to write a quick response email. But in the past I didn't use AI for that because of the obvious AI tells.

Using an editor like this, you get another hidden benefit. Every hand edit you make is tracked, and can be exported at the end of your session. Which means over time you accumulate a series of files that have the diffs between what an AI wrote and how you corrected it. This is incredible data for tone of voice analysis and instruction.

This is just an open source passion project, so I'd love to see how you would make it better. I've been using this tool pretty much non-stop lately, and I've gotten it to a point that it's pretty nice to use, but as soon as you hand it to someone else they'll find something obvious to improve!

Code is available here on my github, so have a look and customize to your needs! Let me know what you end up adding!

Help other people find the tool by starring the repo! Thanks!

(Article written collaboratively with AI, including 248 human comments/edits.)

title: FloatLib: Verified Floating-Point Arithmetic in Lean
description: Arbitrary precision, custom formats, and fast software backends with Lean proofs connecting execution to the specification.
fullText:
Verified Floating-Point Arithmetic in Lean

 Robert Joseph George1,*,
 Will Adkisson2,*,
 Anima Anandkumar1

 1California Institute of Technology
 2Washington University in St. Louis

 Paper
 Code
 Guide

 Overview
 FloatLib is a verified arbitrary-precision floating-point arithmetic library
 in Lean. It supports IEEE binary and decimal, arbitrary-width posits, P3109,
 small ML formats, and user-defined formats and rounding rules. Each certified
 software backend is proved equal to its encoded specification, including
 signed zeros and exceptional values. We built FloatLib to support verified
 machine learning and numerical software with efficient arithmetic.

 Key contributions

 Custom formats and rounding rules. Choose exponent and
 fraction widths, bias, and encoding policies, or define a new representation.
 IEEE binary and decimal, small ML formats, arbitrary-width posits, and P3109
 share interfaces for arithmetic and mixed-format operations.
 Numerical proofs connected to code. Correct rounding,
 half-ulp error bounds, and Sterbenz's lemma describe the arithmetic a program
 executes. Posits also have exact quire accumulation within capacity and
 real-rounding proofs for roots, powers, exponentials, and logarithms.
 Signed zeros, NaNs, infinities, and exception flags.
 The IEEE model makes their encodings and behavior explicit. Proofs about
 complete result words preserve distinctions that equality over the reals
 cannot express.
 Fast certified execution. The planner chooses among
 lookup tables, machine-word kernels, and limb algorithms. Every certified
 choice proves agreement with the same specification; Lean erases proof
 terms during compilation.

 Performance
 We benchmarked six arithmetic operations from 2 to 4,096 bits. The
 guide
 gives all timings and the separate P3109 comparison.

title: Meta's Muse Is Better at Surveilling Than Helping Me
description: The Muse app continues Meta’s trend of opting users into data collection for AI training. It also nudges you to share your bank account, email, and passport information.
fullText:
latest app, Muse, cross-promoted on another Meta-owned platform, Instagram, and decided to download the AI assistant.

“Hand off everyday tasks like finding deals, booking reservations, and managing your inbox,” the pop-up read. “Muse keeps working while you get on with your day.” It’s free to use, and easily connects to other data sources, like my email and bank account. Muse’s default avatar is a beige-colored cross between an Ewok and a Labubu, with its arms outstretched, presumably to scoop up all my data.

Meta’s Muse is a mainstream version of AI agents already popular in Silicon Valley for automating personal tasks, like OpenClaw and Instinct. It’s a hit for the company: the Muse app has been downloaded over 900,000 times in its first week, according to Sensor Tower. The user experience is less like prompting a chatbot, and more like texting a friend with task requests—the AI agent acknowledges messages with a thumbs-up emoji and gets to work in the background. Muse is also available through Meta’s WhatsApp platform.

But after a few days with Muse, I’m convinced this AI tool is more obsessed with collecting data about me than actually getting stuff done.

“Muse is the first personal AI agent built for everyone, with built-in protections and user controls that put people absolutely in charge of how they use it—any suggestion we didn’t build with that in mind from the beginning is ludicrous,” Meta spokesperson Emil Vazquez tells WIRED.

Muse’s ability to surf the web is genuinely impressive. When you ask it to complete a task, Muse uses a “virtual machine” to browse the internet on your behalf, running searches and clicking around on different web pages. When I tested similar tools last year, like the now-defunct ChatGPT Agent, the AI’s clicks were erratic and error-filled. Muse rarely seems to get lost while browsing.

For example, I asked Muse to order breakfast from a local bakery called Kahnfections. It’s a popular spot for tourists visiting San Francisco, so I requested one of the most-purchased options for pick-up. Muse visited the bakery’s website and added a biscuit sandwich with garlic aioli, cheddar cheese, egg, and bacon to my cart.

I was asked to add a credit card via the Stripe payment processor so my agent could complete the purchase. “One tweak the site forced: cheese is single-select, so I picked cheddar and left a note asking them to add Swiss too if they can,” read Muse’s explanation of the breakfast order when it asked for my final approval. Notably, Muse selected the “no tip” option. A bit rude! (I ended up walking down to the shop, ordering something random and delicious.)

title: 'Blatant violation' of rights: News outlets file lawsuit over Trump ban
description:
A growing list of news organizations has announced that they will not publish photographs from the White House on Monday in response to President Trump's move last week to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from covering him or his administration in person. 
The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced Monday afternoon that they were joining the four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — in refusing to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events. 
As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide. 
Later in the day, the White House announced the creation of Trump TV, though details on what the service might include weren't provided. 
The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.
fullText:
A growing list of news organizations has announced that they will not publish photographs from the White House on Monday in response to President Trump's move last week to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico reporters from covering him or his administration in person.

The Washington Post, the New York Times and HuffPost each announced Monday afternoon that they were joining the four major TV networks — ABC, CBS, NBC and Fox News — in refusing to participate in the White House pool, the rotating group of reporters, photographers and videographers that document the president's public events.

As a result, Trump was largely inaudible during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for the White House's new helipad on Monday, where he gave a brief speech without the microphone that the pool would typically provide.

Later in the day, the White House announced the creation of Trump TV, though details on what the service might include weren't provided.

The three banned news organizations filed a lawsuit against Trump and three of his top advisers in federal court earlier Monday, demanding that access for their reporters be immediately restored.

"This morning, we notified the government that we are filing a lawsuit today to protect our First Amendment rights and defend the principle that the government does not decide what the press reports or publishes," CNN, MS NOW and Politico said in a joint statement. "Without notice or process, the White House revoked our journalists' credentials because it objected to our reporting. Left unchallenged, this threatens press freedom and the public's right to independent journalism free from government interference."

CNN had been scheduled to serve as the television pool on Monday. According to Politico, the four other major TV networks are declining to participate in White House pool duties moving forward in response to the ban.

According to the complaint filed in U.S. District Court in Washington, D.C., the news outlets allege that Trump and the White House are retaliating against them for coverage they dislike.

"President Trump has said in no uncertain terms that he would prefer only to be covered by news organizations and reporters who praise his administration," the complaint states. "But the Constitution does not allow a president or any other government official to deprive the press of their First Amendment rights and liberty and property interests with no notice or process based solely on his dislike of the content of their reporting."

The organizations argue that their reporters were not afforded due process and are asking a federal judge to quickly rule that Trump's ban is unconstitutional. The filing cites a 1977 ruling by the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, which found that the White House cannot arbitrarily deny a journalist a press pass without due process.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the filing states.

Trump appeared to respond to the lawsuit in a social media post early Monday.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America," the president wrote on Truth Social. "It is corrupt, purposeful, pervasive, fully coordinated, and totally out of control. It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!"

The White House released a statement on Monday afternoon, saying that access for journalists is "a privilege — not a right."

"The First Amendment protects their right to publish; it does not entitle them to a hard pass, briefing room seat, or place in the press pool," the statement read. "No President is required to host a hostile operation on the grounds. Access has always been a privilege — and President Trump is applying that rule."

On Friday afternoon, Trump announced the ban in a Truth Social post, saying it was not prompted by any particular stories but was "a result of their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

"It's really just cumulative stories over the last few years. You get sick of it," Trump said at an Oval Office event an hour later while explaining his decision to enact "the ban on the free press."

"There's something wrong with a country that can allow people to write purposely negative stories," the president said. "If they want to write them, that's fine, but I don't have to let them into my, into the people's house."

According to CNN, Trump's close aide Natalie Harp showed him clips of media coverage shortly before he announced the ban.

On Saturday, reporters from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were turned away from the White House by members of the Secret Service and had their credentials — so-called hard passes needed for access — confiscated.

The journalists — CNN's Betsy Klein, MS NOW's Akayla Gardner and Politico's Cheyenne Haslett — are listed as plaintiffs in the court filing.

The White House Correspondents' Association condemned the move, saying it violates the First Amendment.

"The American people, through a free and independent press, must be able to scrutinize those elected to power, regardless of whether government officials view it favorably," Jacqui Heinrich, Fox News senior White House correspondent and WHCA president, said in a statement. "That's why courts have repeatedly held that once the White House provides access to journalists, it cannot deny that access arbitrarily or based on the content of their reporting."

On Sunday, Trump posted what appeared to be an AI-generated image of trash bags bearing the logos of CNN, MSNBC (MS NOW's former name) and Politico outside the White House.

The three news outlets are longstanding members of the White House press pool that provides rotating coverage of the administration and travels with the president.

The daily guidance issued by the White House for Monday listed no primary TV pool, identifying Hearst and Real America's Voice as the "secondary" TV crews for the president's events in Washington and his scheduled trip to New York City for the United Nations General Assembly. Trump is scheduled to meet with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and French President Emmanuel Macron on Monday afternoon.

U.S. presidents throughout history have complained about negative coverage of their administrations. In 2009, the Obama administration sought to exclude Fox News from a series of interviews with a Treasury Department official in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, but backed down when the other major television networks objected.

Trump, however, has continued his adversarial relationship with the media, often referring to the press as the "enemy of the people."

In 2018, Trump administration officials revoked the press pass of then-CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta after they said that he had interrupted the president during a news conference. The network sued, and a federal judge ordered Acosta's credentials restored.

A similar situation played out the following year when the White House revoked Playboy correspondent Brian Karem's press pass over a verbal argument between Karem and Sebastian Gorka, a former White House aide, at a Rose Garden event. A federal judge ordered the White House to restore Karem's pass.

Last year, Trump barred Associated Press journalists from the Oval Office, Air Force One and some official events after the news service declined to refer to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name, the Gulf of America. The AP filed suit and the case is ongoing.

In his first event without a network TV pool on Monday, Trump unveiled the White House's new helipad before departing for New York. His remarks were nearly inaudible on the White House video feed. Joe Reberkenny, a White House correspondent for the Washington Blade who was serving as the in-town pool reporter, said he couldn't hear Trump "over the sound of the helicopter."

title: State of emergency declared in California ahead of possibly historic El Niño
description:
Governor Newsom speaking into a microphone at an event, wearing a white collared shirt
Gavin Newsom, the governor of California, declared a state of emergency for the entire state on Monday morning ahead of what is likely to become a historic El Niño. 
"I find that conditions of extreme peril to the safety of persons and property exist due to the developing El Niño event," the declaration states. 
This state of emergency is not an announcement that an emergency is already ongoing, but a statement of preparation for the storms that are ahead this winter. 
The declaration mobilizes state-level resources to support local mitigation and recovery efforts, while streamlining the procurement of resources needed to prepare for El Niño's impacts.
“We are not waiting for this season’s storms to be on our doorstep,” said Cal OES Director Caroline Thomas Jacobs in a statement from the governor's office.

title: Iran threatens ‘new weapons’ as Trump weighs meeting with its president
description:
Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend. 
“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.
Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.
fullText:
Iran warned Monday it would use “new weapons with new capabilities” if the U.S. launched a fresh assault after President Donald Trump ramped up the rhetoric against Tehran over the weekend.

“If a new aggression takes place, we will definitely change the weapons and geography of the war,” Hossein Mohebbi, a spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Monday, according to the semiofficial Fars news agency.

Mohebbi did not provide details on what the new weapons were or which new locations could be hit.

Earlier, Trump said he would “probably” be open to meeting with his Iranian counterpart, President Masoud Pezeshkian, during the United Nations General Assembly this week, Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst reported Sunday.

The possibility of a meeting offered a glimmer of hope for a resolution to the nearly seven-month war with Iran, which has resulted in Iran blocking the key Strait of Hormuz, and its Yemeni allies bombing a crucial east-west oil pipeline and threatening another crucial waterway. Resultant economic shock waves have hit the U.S. and the world economy, driving up oil and diesel prices and fueling inflation.

Trump also said he was still deciding how to proceed with the war, describing his options as “wiping Iran out, letting them rot economically, or making a deal.”

“My question is, if and when do I blow the entire nation up,” he said.

“They better behave,” Trump warned.

The president has previously said he did not believe the Iran war would end until after November’s midterm elections. He has also said oil prices would not come down until then.

Oil prices slid to their lowest point in more than a week Monday as hopes for renewed talks between the U.S. and Iran grew, while signs of a recovery in Saudi crude exports eased supply concerns, despite continued attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis.

Trump told Fox News that Washington was in constant communication with the Houthis — and that the Yemeni rebel group had agreed not to fight with the U.S., Yingst reported.

Trump has said that the administration had been in touch with the Houthis, but did not say when.

“The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through.”

Violence escalated over the weekend, with the Houthis saying they had used missiles and drones to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh on Saturday, as well as an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

Meanwhile, fighting flared in southwest Yemen as the rebel group made gains against Saudi-backed forces.

The New York Times reported Monday that the president had considered, but ultimately decided against on Sunday joining Saudi Arabia in joint strikes against the Houthis in Yemen.

NBC News was not immediately able to independently confirm the newspaper’s reporting. The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

“This is a really fluid situation,” Adam Baron, a fellow at the New America think tank who follows Yemen and the wider Gulf region, said Monday.

He cautioned that he would not “rule out anything” when it comes to Trump’s stance on whether to help Saudi Arabia in its fight against the Houthis.

Shipping data showed 17 commodity vessels passed through the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 37 a week earlier, though Middle Eastern producers continue to export oil on tankers with their transponders off, Reuters reported.

A total of 22 tankers, mainly very large crude carriers, or VLCCs, exited Hormuz in the week of Sept. 13, with Saudi Arabia and Iraq each accounting for 43% of the volume, the outlet reported, citing data from tracking group Kpler, which maintains the MarineTraffic website.

Meanwhile, at least 51 vessels made the crossing along the Bab el Mandeb, with 33 vessels exiting the waterway over the weekend as the Houthis tightened their grip over the strait, the outlet reported. That was down from 57 vessels in the previous weekend.

The Yemeni Health and Environment Ministry accused Saudi Arabia of launching airstrikes targeting telecommunications towers in the Khabb wa ash-Sha’af district of Al-Jawf Governorate on Sunday that killed four telecommunications workers and injured three others.

“Targeting essential service infrastructure, including telecommunications towers, constitutes a flagrant violation of international and humanitarian laws,” the ministry said in a post on Telegram. “It reveals the aggressor’s determination to disrupt basic services and exacerbate the suffering of the Yemeni people,” it said.

The spread of the AI-powered systems to provide help about the provision of vital services such as energy, banking, phones and internet, is making it harder for millions of already digitally excluded people to handle snags, according to the frontline charity that last year provided more than 2.7 million people with one-on-one help in England and Wales.

fullText:
Citizens Advice says providers of essential services such as energy, banking, phone and internet should guarantee the ‘right to talk to a human’

Stop relying on AI chatbots for customer care and guarantee the “right to talk to a human”, Citizens Advice has urged essential service providers, as research found they wasted time, caused stress and delayed problem solving for more than half of users.

The spread of the AI-powered systems to provide help about the provision of vital services such as energy, banking, phones and internet, is making it harder for millions of already digitally excluded people to handle snags, according to the frontline charity that last year provided more than 2.7 million people with one-on-one help in England and Wales.

The charity concluded that chatbots caused harm, saying too often they trapped humans in an “endless loop” in which nothing got resolved, and almost half of people who had to use a chatbot found them unhelpful, with some concluding the chatbot seemed rigged to “make me give up”.

It called for service providers to respect a new right for customers to speak to a human after it investigated the wider impact of digital exclusion, estimated to affect at least 14 million UK citizens. It uncovered slower and less reliable support for people who struggle with or have limited access to online systems and found the erosion of phone, face-to-face and paper communication had created a two-tier support system.

“Going round in circles with a chatbot isn’t just annoying, it can be a blockade to essential services,” said Tom MacInnes, policy director at Citizens Advice. “We’ve seen organisations’ overreliance on chatbots and online forms leaving people unable to fix billing problems, sort out their debt or even access homelessness prevention services. There’s a role for chatbots, but the quiet erosion of face-to-face and telephone services is letting too many people fall through the cracks.”

That erosion of traditional ways of communicating means that people without good digital access can face serious difficulties getting simple problems fixed. For example, the charity found that submitting energy meter readings to correct a wrong bill can take less than an hour online if systems are working properly. Without good digital access it takes as long as six weeks offline, putting people “at risk of further harm”. In some locations applying for low-cost social tariff broadband – itself intended to reduce digital exclusion – is being made harder by being digital only, Citizens Advice found after it took evidence from its frontline advisers and hundreds of case summaries.

One adviser reported that when people struggled with digital-only applications for homelessness support they ended up “homeless for longer … they’re in danger … they’re losing money … they get into debt” and said: “It can ruin a lot of people’s lives.”

The warnings come amid growing frustration with the proliferation of AI customer services. Online message boards with titles like: “I’m so sick of AI Customer ‘Support” Chat Bots” and “Has anyone ever actually had their problem solved by a company’s chatbot?” are filled with tales of woe. Several chronicle frustrated customers’ attempts to circumvent phone-based chatbots by repeatedly yelling “human!”.

Only 20% of UK adults polled on behalf of Citizens Advice in July said chatbots were their preferred way to communicate, with phone calls, email and instant messaging all preferred.

Gripes about other forms of digital exclusion include multifactor authentication, which requires rapid and dextrous manipulation of more than one device just to log in and time-limits to complete transactions.

Of the people who found it difficult or not possible to talk to a human to resolve an issue with their essential services, 49% felt stress or frustration, 27% felt powerless, 44% experienced delays to resolution and 14% gave up trying to resolve the issue altogether.

The UK government has previously said it is investing £11.9m in a digital inclusion innovation fund, supporting local projects to help people get online. About 1.7m households in the UK do not have a laptop, tablet or desktop computer.

A government spokesperson said: “Businesses have a legal obligation to provide contact information in a manner which is clear and easily accessible.”

WASHINGTON, Sept 21 (Reuters) - Critics swiftly decried a California-driven settlement with Paramount Skydance that cleared the way for its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery, saying it will hurt competition in Hollywood, failed to protect jobs and lacks substantial ‌concessions from the media conglomerate.

Opponents of the merger accused California Attorney General Rob Bonta and Governor Gavin Newsom of caving to wealthy interests, particularly ‌Paramount CEO David Ellison, after Paramount threatened to leave the state if the lawsuit was not dropped.

"Today, billionaires have yet again bribed, censored, and bullied their way to the top," said Alvaro Bedoya, ​a former member of the US Federal Trade Commission and adviser at the American Economic Liberties Project. "Layoffs will follow. People from L.A. to Atlanta will lose their jobs, small businesses will lose their contracts, your cable bill and movie ticket will be even more expensive."

Disappointment with the settlement rippled beyond Hollywood, illustrating a growing split in the Democratic Party between moderates, who are more business-friendly, and progressives, who seek a harder line to deliver affordability for US consumers.

US Senator Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from ‌Massachusetts, criticized the deal, and said Paramount is a "clear candidate ⁠for antitrust scrutiny in a future pro-competition administration."

"This settlement greenlights an anti-monopoly disaster that will result in higher prices and fewer jobs, and enables a handful of billionaires to call the shots in the American media," she said.

Bonta, in a press conference on Monday, said the settlement is "not a vote of support" of the acquisition, because "it does not serve competition well." But he also argued it would amount to more production in California.

Ellison said on Monday that the deal will strengthen competition and benefit consumers and workers.

Spokespeople for Paramount and Bonta did not immediately respond to requests ​for ​comment on the reaction by critics of the deal.

Bonta had said from the outset that ​structural remedies, where a company sells off part of its ‌business, are superior to promises to change or uphold business practices.

Yet the settlement does not require Paramount to sell off any cable channels, or any component of what Bonta said made Paramount and Warner such a formidable combo in theatrical film distribution, such as its lucrative intellectual property.

fullText:
As college costs and student debt have Americans doubting the value of higher education, there's growing interest in high-paying jobs that don't require a degree - and in public policy supporting training for them. But six-figure jobs that skip a bachelor's degree do require more than a high school diploma and remain rare, according to an analysis released Monday by Niche, a higher education platform.

The highest salaries for workers without a bachelor's degree are typically in jobs gated by federal certification or specialized training, including commercial pilots, air traffic controllers, elevator installers and nuclear reactor operators, the study shows.

The findings counter an emerging narrative about the prevalence of six-figure jobs in the skilled trades that don't require higher education. Politicians and business leaders have touted careers in electrical work, HVAC and plumbing earning more than $100,000, arguing that a four-year degree is unnecessary for financial security.

While those jobs offer healthy salaries, research shows their median earnings are more modest than salaries for less common occupations that don't require a bachelor's degree.

Using data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics, Niche economist Allison Shrivastava found that only 9.4 percent of occupations with a median wage of $100,000 or more don't require a bachelor's degree. Those occupations account for just 0.3 percent of 13.8 million annual openings projected across every occupation in which a bachelor's is not a prerequisite.

There are four times as many openings that do not require a bachelor's degree, but the jobs generally pay less. On average, the median earnings for those occupations are around $45,000 a year, compared with $96,000 for job openings seeking people with a bachelor's degree, according to the analysis.

"There's a little bit of romanticizing the trades," Shrivastava said. "There are some trade jobs that you can make six figures right out the gate, but they are more the exception than the rule."

She said that doesn't discount the power vocational training has to lift people out of poverty and provide economic success. But those workers have less earning potential than people with a bachelor's degree, and can have a harder time finding work in other fields without additional training, Shrivastava said.

A study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research found the college wage premium - the extra pay degree holders make compared to workers with only a high school diploma - doubles over a worker's lifetime, from 27 percent at age 25 to 60 percent at age 55. Workers with college degrees obtain jobs in professions with greater scope for on-the-job training and wage growth, according to the study.

The meeting was the latest cordial encounter between the Republican president and a democratic socialist mayor, who have struck up a surprisingly warm relationship despite their lack of political overlap, and have tried to find common ground in helping the city they both love.
fullText:
NEW YORK (AP) — President Donald Trump's trip to New York for a speech at the United Nations started Monday with a detour to Gracie Mansion for an hourlong chat — and a trip down memory lane — with Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

The president, appearing with Mamdani after their meeting, reminisced about his previous visits to the official residence of the city's mayors and recalled "great ones and some not so great ones" who have led the city in the past.

"Hopefully you're going to be a great one," he said, giving Mamdani a pat on the back. "And you're off to a start."

The meeting was the latest cordial encounter between the Republican president and a democratic socialist mayor, who have struck up a surprisingly warm relationship despite their lack of political overlap, and have tried to find common ground in helping the city they both love.

With scores of world leaders arriving in the city for the United Nations General Assembly, there Trump stood beside Mamdani on the lawn of the custard-yellow mayoral mansion in Manhattan.

"I have a lot of meetings right now, very important meetings with heads of different countries, but this is like a little bit of old home week for me," Trump said, adding "We've done so many things from the beautiful home or house or building standing right behind me."

Trump and Mamdani told reporters they discussed a potential housing project in the borough of Queens and how to make New York more affordable for the working class.

They have met at least twice previously and have appeared to maintain some level of contact with one another, though the mayor stays tightlipped about any ongoing conversations with the president.

The pair of polarizing leaders first gathered in the Oval Office shortly after Mamdani's election victory last year for a surprisingly cordial confab that centered on ways to help their shared hometown, a detente that came after months of verbal sparring.

A few months later in February, Mamdani again took a quick jaunt to Washington to present Trump with a mock New York Daily News front page that said "Trump to City: Let's Build," as he pitched new housing investments in the city.

As they did after their first Oval Office meeting, Trump and Mamdani acknowledged their political and policy differences while standing side by side.

Mamdani was asked about Trump's decision to bar certain news outlets from the White House, with the mayor saying it was important that those networks, and others, be present for the Gracie Mansion event. Trump then defended his restrictions on the news organizations whose coverage he called biased.

"It's interesting because they said they were gonna boycott me. But they never boycott me," the president said, before adding, "I think that these outlets have an obligation to be fair."

Trump's previous visits to Gracie Mansion included attending the 2003 wedding of former Mayor Rudy Giuliani and a 2007 book party for former Democratic U.S. Rep. Charles Rangel.

After Trump left, Mamdani returned to the lawn to answer a few more questions, telling reporters that he and the president have sharp disagreements but that the relationship has endured nevertheless.

"I will continue to have conversations with the president, and frankly, anyone who can deliver relief to the people of this city," Mamdani said.

title: Trump called off Houthi strikes as military leaders debated risks of expanding war
description:
President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office of the White House last week. (Samuel Corum / Bloomberg via Getty Images)
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON — U.S. military leaders are divided on whether President Donald Trump should get involved with the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, according to two U.S. officials.

The Saudis have been asking Trump for the U.S. military to take action against the Houthis, a request that grew more urgent in recent days as the rebels claimed they shot down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet and were quickly advancing on Marib province, which is home to Yemen’s largest oil and gas fields.

Some military leaders are making the case within the Pentagon and to Trump administration officials that opening another military front in the region is a bad idea amid concerns about the Pentagon’s dwindling supply of defensive and long-range weaponry, while noting that the Houthis are not striking U.S. ships, the U.S. officials said.

Yet other military leaders are arguing in favor of strikes, saying the U.S. should help Riyadh retaliate for Houthi strikes in Saudi Arabia and the claim of downing of the F-15 — a challenge to Saudi air superiority over Yemen, the officials said. They said these military leaders are privately expressing concern that for the U.S. not to act more forcefully is a betrayal of an important regional ally.

Trump had ordered strikes against the Houthis to begin around 5 p.m. Eastern Standard Time on Sunday, but the military was notified shortly after 2 p.m. on Sunday that the order was canceled, the two U.S. officials said. One of the officials said Trump has not taken military action off the table in the future.

One senior U.S. military leader in the region specifically warned that action against the Houthis could create unmitigated risk to U.S. troops in Middle East and the Iran war mission, including a U.S. naval blockade and security operations in the Strait of Hormuz, the two U.S. officials said. They said the military leader also made clear that U.S. forces could carry out the Iran mission and strikes against the Houthis and mitigate some of the risks, the officials said.

The internal divide underscores the bind the president is increasingly in as the U.S. remains locked in a war with Iran that he began but has struggled to end, and faces a shortage of key weaponry. The Saudis have been a critical U.S. ally in the Middle East, including throughout the war with Iran. Trump told Fox News over the weekend that he’s deciding whether to escalate the war with Iran, a position he has articulated on and off over the past few months.

The White House and a spokesperson for the Saudi Embassy in Washington, D.C., did not respond to a request for comment. The Pentagon declined to comment.

There has already been tension between the U.S. and its Middle East allies over the war. In May, Saudi Arabia was surprised by an announcement by Trump to help ships through the Strait of Hormuz and suspended the U.S. military’s ability to use its bases and airspace. Trump abruptly reversed his decision.

The U.S. has already been supporting the Saudis by sharing intelligence, helping with planning, sending military advisers forward with the Saudi forces and even providing some logistical support, NBC News has reported. But the Saudis have repeatedly asked the U.S. to do more, including help with strikes against the Houthis.

Trump had not shown interest in acting until Thursday, when Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman told him in a phone call that the kingdom cannot succeed alone and after a series of developments — including the Houthis targeting Saudi infrastructure, downing the F-15 and threatening to take control of Yemen’s oil industry, according to one of the U.S. officials.

After the call, Trump ordered the military to provide him with fresh options for strikes against the Houthis, the official said. Chairman of the Joint Chiefs Dan Caine called a 6 p.m. emergency meeting in The Tank, the top-security conference room in the Pentagon, to discuss options, the official said, canceling a trip to Copenhagen to meet with NATO chiefs of defense.

U.S. military officials have presented Trump with options for degrading Houthi military capabilities and stopping the rebels’ recent advances several times since Thursday, the official said, adding that the Pentagon has enough assets in the region to be ready to act if ordered to do so.

The New York Times reported some details of Trump’s decision-making process.

Violence escalated over the weekend, as the Houthis said they’d used missiles and drones on Saturday to attack “sensitive” sites in ‌Riyadh and an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, a key oil export hub.

The spokesperson for the coalition forces issued a statement on Saturday saying Saudi Arabia had successfully intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile launched toward Riyadh and that the Houthis “target civilians and civilian infrastructure in the capital.”

The militant group also made a rapid advance to control the Bab el Mandeb Strait on the Red Sea, yet another oil chokepoint. The advance has posed a major challenge for the Saudis, who rely on that shipping route particularly since the Strait of Hormuz has been largely shuttered during the Iran war.

The Houthis took control of Yemen in a bloody civil war in 2014 against a Saudi-backed coalition. A fragile truce between the Houthis and the Yemeni government backed by the U.N. was reached in 2022.

Trump announced a ceasefire with the Houthis last year after weeks of punishing strikes against the militant group. Under the deal, the U.S. suspended military action and the Houthis stopped attacking U.S. ships.

Trump recently has said his administration has had discussions with the Houthis but has not offered details. “The Houthis called us, and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said earlier this month. “They would much prefer not having us involved.”
